Amazon is gaining ground in grocery thanks to items like fresh shrimp and berries. Roughly a year after expanding same-day fresh grocery delivery to thousands of cities and towns in the US, Amazon's perishable grocery sales are booming — and taking market share from traditional retailers, according to data from market research firm Nielsen IQ. Sales of groceries such as seafood, dairy, and produce on Amazon increased severalfold between June and August, per Nielsen IQ's data. Amazon also posted market share gains in the food category for the year through late August as traditional grocery stores lost it, Nielsen found. "Shoppers are increasingly embracing Amazon for categories that historically represented one of the largest barriers to online grocery adoption," Nielsen wrote in its report. Amazon has spent years trying to break into grocery, though it hasn't hit a home run in the category as it did with books or cloud computing. The company acquired Whole Foods, opened and shuttered another brick-and-mortar grocery chain, and created a selection of private-label groceries, among other steps. The Nielsen IQ data suggest that Amazon's latest push — toward delivering fresh groceries quickly across much of the US — is yielding some results in the competitive grocery space. Many of the shoppers buying fresh foods on Amazon come from households with incomes over $100,000 and tend to be older, according to Nielsen IQ. They also tend to be frequent Amazon users, placing more orders and spending more money on the platform than an average user. That means fresh groceries, one of the most frequent purchases for US households, are "a potentially important lever for increasing shopper frequency and overall spend" on Amazon, the report reads. To keep the momentum going, Amazon will need to take on formidable rivals. One is Walmart, which already uses its stores and its own army of gig workers to deliver groceries same-day. A hot, new beauty treatment driving tens of millions of dollars in sales around the globe is now aiming for the US market. Its unusual ingredient: skin from dead Americans. Each year, tens of thousands of Americans donate bodily tissue upon their deaths, generally by checking a box at a motor vehicle department or through an authorization made by a loved one. Over the past few years, tens of millions of dollars' worth of donated skin has traveled from American tissue banks to biotech companies in South Korea, the beauty capital of the world. There, among other uses, it is turned into injectable beauty treatments. The maker of the market-leading Korean brand said last week it has signed a distribution contract to introduce its skin-derived injection to the US market next year. It isn't clear whether the product can be sold in the US without approval from federal regulators. Business Insider traced the tissue supply chain to understand how donor tissue from, say, San Antonio can end up for sale at a clinic in Seoul — and how much money is being made along the way. People who donate tissue "have no idea of how much money is changing hands in the course of all of this," Ana Iltis, a professor at Wake Forest and former president of the American Society for Bioethics and Humanities, told Business Insider. "With tissue donation, there's a lot of money at stake." Donors and their families can't be paid for organ or tissue donations under US law. For decades, American plastic surgeons have used products made from human tissue for skin grafts and reconstructive surgeries. That practice includes aesthetic uses — such as cartilage for a nose job or skin for a breast augmentation — though many doctors prefer to use the patient's own tissue for such procedures. Now, skincare treatments made from human tissue can be purchased for a few hundred dollars and administered at a med spa or dermatology clinic in under an hour. In South Korea, a mecca for cutting-edge beauty treatments, at least 10 biotech companies are making or planning to introduce skin-derived injections. They are the latest generation of a treatment known among beauty obsessives as "skin boosters." Get your algorithm just right, and your social-media feeds will soon be full of before-and-afters showing off the purported benefits of these products. They depict patients, typically women and sometimes young ones, going from dull to dewy, fine-lined to smooth. If one of your loved ones donated tissue or you have worked in tissue recovery and processing, Business Insider wants to hear from you. You can reach Madeline Berg at mberg@businessinsider.com or 914-420-4721, and Jack Newsham at jnewsham@businessinsider.com or at 314-971-1627. This year, the skin-derived injections are projected to generate $75 million in sales in South Korea, according to analysts at Yuanta Securities. No brand is bigger than Re2O, which one dermatologist on Instagram called "the Love Potion No. 9 for cells." It accounts for between 60% and 70% of sales in the category, according to L&C Bio, its manufacturer. Re2O notched the equivalent of more than $17 million in sales in the first half of this year, helping swing the company to an operating profit of about $11 million after a loss of about $326,000 in the same period last year, L&C Bio said. It has expanded the product line with Re2O Fine, marketed for more delicate skin, and is planning to launch a human fat-derived filler next year. The company said it sold 700,000 units of Re2O as of September. It is available in Singapore and China, and has been approved in the United Arab Emirates, Peru, and Thailand. Last week, L&C Bio said that it has signed a contract to deliver at least $60 million of Re2O to the US over the next five years. The company also said it may explore acquiring US tissue banks with its US distribution partner. L&C Bio's plan to introduce Re2O to the US could spark a regulatory showdown. L&C Bio has said Re2O falls into a category of products such as skin grafts that don't require approval from the US Food and Drug Administration. Some products that manufacturers claim qualify to be sold under this category don't actually meet the applicable criteria, the FDA told Business Insider. The agency said it wouldn't discuss any specific products under investigation. "Products derived from donor skin that have been decellularized, dried, and ground into a powder for injection as a cosmetic 'skin booster' may raise significant questions" and may have to go through a more complex regulatory approval process, the agency said. L&C Bio said it wouldn't comment on its discussions with regulators. Re2O's biggest competitor, CellREDM, came onto the South Korean market in late 2025. It has been such a success that in the quarter ended June 30, operating income for its maker, Hans Biomed, soared to over $3 million after barely eking out a profit in the year-earlier period. "In the human tissue business, access to raw materials is the lifeblood of the industry," L&C Bio's founder and CEO, Whan Chul Lee, said in Korean in a February interview with a South Korean news outlet. For his company and its competitors, that lifeblood flows from the United States. Roughly 90% of all the human tissue used in South Korea is imported, according to South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety. Less than 4% of South Korean adults are registered to donate organs, and even fewer donate tissue. Korean biotech companies have turned primarily to the US, where well over half of adults are registered donors. Cadaver skin is collected in the US by organ procurement organizations, known as OPOs, and tissue banks. In the transplant system, skin is treated as a tissue, not an organ. After tissue is collected, its route can vary. A nonprofit OPO often transfers it to an American tissue bank. The tissue bank pays a fee to the OPO, depending on factors like the amount and quality of tissue recovered. The fee covers the cost of the tissue recovery as well as a margin that supports other programs offered by the OPO. Tissue banks — which can be nonprofit or for-profit entities — supply donor skin to Korean biotech firms. Much of the US skin supplied to South Korea is used for more traditional medical purposes, like skin grafts for burn victims. L&C Bio makes such therapeutic products and says it prioritizes supply for them. L&C Bio spent more than $25 million on donor skin from US tissue banks between 2023 and 2025 and $3.8 million in the first half of this year, according to corporate filings. The company told Business Insider that a quarter of its skin supply is used to make Re2O. Organ distribution is coordinated by a public-private partnership with the federal government. Tissue is handled differently. It is distributed through commercial relationships. The more traditional business aspects of the tissue industry have been a subject of debate since the federal law governing America's organ recovery and distribution system was enacted in the 1980s. In a system that relies on altruism, money changing hands could affect public trust, Jerold Mande, who helped write the National Organ Transplant Act, told Business Insider. There is little data on American attitudes toward tissue donation. A survey of more than 1,000 families of donors in the US published in a 2010 academic journal found less than 30% said they thought it was acceptable for donated tissues to be processed and distributed by for-profit companies. Revenue from tissue, primarily skin and bone, drove 93% of American OPO profits between 2013 and 2017, or a total of about $107 million per year in profit at 51 OPOs, according to a study in the medical journal Transplantation. The Association of Organ Procurement Organizations called the study outdated, said the money collected for tissue helps fund other life-saving work, and objected to the study's use of the word "profit." "Reimbursed funds go directly back into the organization, supporting organ procurement as well as aftercare programs for donor families such as bereavement support and grief counseling," said Jenny Daigle, a spokesperson for the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations. Organizations must have a margin and reserves to remain financially stable, she added. Human tissue donations help millions of people in the US each year, including skin for burn victims, bone for cancer survivors, and eyes for the visually impaired, Daigle said. Regenerative Biologics, a Florida tissue bank, provides all the skin for Re2O, L&C Bio confirmed to Business Insider. Regenerative's CEO, Sandy McCann, said her tissue bank acts as an intermediary, supplying skin collected by other organizations, and provides L&C Bio only with skin from donors who have given consent for international and cosmetic use. If other American tissue banks have skin that they can't use, "many times we can place it where someone can," she said. Regenerative had just over $16 million in annual revenue in 2024 and 2025, according to reports filed with a Florida regulator. By reviewing South Korean government records and images of product packaging, Business Insider identified two other US tissue banks, South Texas Blood and Tissue and RTI Surgical, that supply tissue for skin-derived injectable beauty treatments made by Korean companies. South Texas Blood & Tissue supplies skin used to make South Korea's No. 2 brand, CellREDM. The tissue bank is based in San Antonio, sometimes called "Military City, USA" because of the large military base there. Educational materials on the tissue bank's website say that donor skin "heals patients suffering from burns or other traumatic wounds, and in reconstructive surgeries, including those wounded during military service." South Texas Blood & Tissue said each of its tissue donors helps an average of 75 recipients. International distribution and commercial use are longstanding practices in the tissue industry, the group said. Tissue donor families have the option to decline cosmetic, international, or research use, the group added. "Our top priority is to serve as good stewards of these tissue donations, and to ensure that all tissue we recover has the greatest impact possible," it said. RTI, a Florida tissue bank that does business as Evergen, said it transfers a small amount of unprocessed donor skin to DOF, a tissue bank in South Korea that manufactures the skin-derived injection product Juveacell. RTI added that it is "dedicated to honoring the generosity of donors and their families." Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe—and boost its faltering economy. However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy. As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations. “We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED. In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility. Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate. The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment. Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.” In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act. Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says. When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.” Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change. The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten. But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns. As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. The real reasons US politicians are getting older Not many US politicians have endured for as long as Hal Rogers, who will go into November's midterm elections seeking his 24th term in the House of Representatives. The 88-year-old Republican has represented Kentucky's 5th congressional district since 1981, making him the longest serving member of the House of Representatives. He was elected on the same night Ronald Reagan won his first presidential term under the slogan "Let's make America great again", a phrase later revived by Donald Trump. Among the challengers Rogers beat to win the nomination this year was one 60 years his junior. But Rogers, born in the 1930s, is far from the only senior US politician to have stuck at the job into their 80s. Others to have done so include US President Donald Trump, 80; Trump's predecessor Joe Biden, who left office at 82; and Nancy Pelosi, who stepped down as the Democratic leader in the House at the same age. Chuck Grassley, 93, is still a senator. He entered politics in 1958, before Alaska and Hawaii were even US states. Hal Rogers, far left, with Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, centre, in 1996 The age and health of some politicians has raised widespread concern within both Republican and Democratic circles, however, reigniting questions about whether age limits or health checks should be imposed. The US is well known for its "gerontocracy", a government ruled by people who are significantly older than most of the adult population. At the other end of the age spectrum, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under the age of 45 among comparable democracies, according to research from the Inter-Parliamentary Union. So why are so few young people becoming politicians? And for those who do enter politics, can they make a success of it? Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November. Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters. When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream. The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans. Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates. Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (Â£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website. Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says. The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56. In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington Mitch McConnell's recent long spell of absence has raised questions But the median age of Congress members has ticked upwards over time. Congressional records show that the lowest median ages in the House and Senate were both recorded in the early 1980s - at 48 and 52 respectively. The average ages of a House member and a senator at the start of the current Congress were 58 and 65 respectively, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center. The median age of a US citizen is 39. There is now also a sharper focus on the health and acuity of some of the nation's oldest politicians. Joe Biden's age became a major issue while he was in office. To a lesser extent Trump has faced questions too.  So too has Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, with increasing regularity, after a months-long absence from Congress to undergo medical treatment. Meanwhile, on the Democratic side, Maxine Waters, 88, faces a leadership challenge as the lead Democrat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee, with her age considered by some to be a factor counting against her. Some of the most vocal critics of this so-called gerontocracy have been candidates who identify as democratic socialists, meaning that their political views are further to the left than those of the Democratic Party mainstream. These candidates tend to campaign heavily on the cost of living and other issues that cut through to Millennials and Gen Z, and their supporters skew younger too. The demographic profile of people who vote tends to skew older, like the elected officials themselves. Pew research highlights that the proportion of non-voters who are young (aged 18 to 29) has been increasing. In the 2020 US election, 25% of non-voters belonged to that age category, according to Pew. Four years later, it had risen to 30%. Pew adds that voters under 30 were underrepresented in 2024. Voters in that age category made up 20% of the voting-eligible population, though accounted for only 15% of all the votes that were actually cast. Campaigners argue that these demographic trends matter because they leave some issues underrepresented. "Yes, that might result in older people being elected, but I think it really skews, too, what issues are important; what issues politicians are incentivised to talk about and to take care of," says Grace Mausser, the co-chair of the New York City wing of the Democratic Socialists of America. Zohran Mamdani has signposted a possible route for younger candidates Mausser campaigned for Zohran Mamdani in his winning bid last year to become, at age 34, New York City's youngest mayor since 1892. Mamdani was held up as an example of a rare youthful success story, but his ally Mausser is less concerned with a politician's age than with their outlook. Mausser says it is not necessarily a problem if someone has been in politics for a long time. Rather, the problem can be what may result from that: "You become so used to the language and the ideas of the political establishment that anything else - any new ideas, whether they come from young people or old people - seem crazy." She invokes left-wing Democratic senator Bernie Sanders, 85, as an example of an older politician with a long tenure on Capitol Hill who has embraced change and had ideas that have resonated across generations. In the US, older people hold politicians in far higher esteem than younger people - even more so than in many other countries, according to a Pew survey from spring 2025. Some 62% of 18-34-year-olds were likely to say few or none of their elected officials are honest, compared with 45% of people aged over 50. Of the 25 countries surveyed by Pew, only Greece's young adults had a more pessimistic view of the honesty of politicians. For one expert who studies political engagement on both sides of the Atlantic, disaffection among young people helps to explain their unwillingness to participate in politics. The issue is not helped by the fact Congress has minimum age requirements for members, he says. Candidates must be 30 to serve as a senator, and 25 to be a representative. "The one leads to another," remarks James Sloam from Royal Holloway, University of London. "If you don't have enough young people engaged in politics generally, then they won't become representatives." What is more, Sloam says, young people in the US and the UK alike are alert to the fact that power does not just lie in politics. They are aware there are many other areas of work in which they can wield influence - including over elected officials. Young voters tend to be less engaged than their older counterparts For those young people who do end up in high-profile political positions, the next question is whether they can make a success of it, especially when it comes to parenthood. Over the summer, the stories of two high-profile young women working in Washington raised fresh questions around compatibility of the job with motherhood. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37, a Democratic congresswoman who took office aged 29, announced that she had started the process of freezing her eggs. Later the same week in August, Karoline Leavitt, 29, who was appointed the youngest ever White House press secretary almost two years earlier, said she would leave the Trump administration to spend more time with her family, including her newborn baby. She explained: "I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of [being] the White House press secretary." Only a handful of women have given birth while elected to Congress, while a few dozen lawmakers are mothers to children under the age of 18. The federal government, like many US employers, does not offer paid parental leave. JD Vance, 42, one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, recently acknowledged that having young children might impact on his own decision to run for the White House in 2028, saying: "We've got four little kids." America's two-party system is cited as another barrier to young people getting involved with politics. Sloam, the London academic, says this is because only a relatively narrow range of views are represented. He highlights research that indicates young people are more energised by social movements or issue-based campaigns than by party politics.  And within party politics, he notes the example of Mamdani and others on the political left who appear to be galvanising youth support outside the Democratic Party mainstream. But he cautions that "it's a little bit sporadic at the moment".  The Republican Party has been through its own splintering over the last decade with the advent of Trump's MAGA movement, which appealed to a swathe of young men in the 2024 presidential election. Some European democracies show a more pluralistic political environment can increase youth engagement, Sloam says. Scandinavian countries, for example, which are more likely to be multi-party, provide a clear counter example because the parties of government in those countries "work with those social movements to try and bring them into the political systems". Citing countries such as Norway, Sloam suggests there is a cycle whereby stronger youth turnout and youth trust in the political system leads to more involvement in politics. It is true that some lawmakers should know when to call it a day, some experts argue, but equally, voters should not lose sight of the qualities of age. Nor should they confuse age with competency. "Age alone is a very poor predictor of anything," says Tracey Gendron, a professor of gerontology at Virginia Commonwealth University whose research challenges the presumption that ageing is always linked to decline. "You can have a 45-year-old who is experiencing depression or substance abuse who may not have the cognition necessary for the job," she says. And equally: "You can have an 85-year-old with incredible integrity and political judgement and wisdom who is fully capable of doing the job." Gendron accepts the point that US politicians are not representative of the nation's age profile, but says this just shows that there are many ways in which Congress could afford to diversify. "It's funny when we call it a gerontocracy and we focus just on age alone," she says. "When you look at most other aspects of representation - gender, sexuality, religion, race - we're not representative there either." Chief Correspondent covering media and technology Derek Thompson writes and talks about a lot of things. But some things pay better than others: "Dimes for analysis, dollars for facts, and Benjamins for facts about artificial intelligence," he tells me. Thompson, a longtime Atlantic writer who left to launch his own Substack in 2025, has an avid following — Barack Obama reportedly reads him to stay on top of AI developments. That following also creates an inherent tension: If he only creates work he knows will have a big audience, it squeezes out other subjects he's passionate about, like the way technology affects the media we consume. Or why he thinks Americans should embrace a pro-building mindset — the subject of "Abundance," the recent book he co-wrote with Ezra Klein. I talked to Thompson about AI — of course — along with some of his other passions, like why he thinks pro sports are a conspiracy that lets the richest people in the world turn "their already-elevated wealth into exospherically extreme wealth." You can hear our entire conversation on my Channels podcast. There are costs to an economic infrastructure project that leans so heavily into data centers that other modes of construction are being starved for resources. Jason Furman, an economist at Harvard, just published a graph showing that in the last year, while data center construction's up by more than 60%, construction of hospitals is down, construction of offices is down, construction of housing is down, construction of just about everything else that you can name, including manufacturing facilities, is down because data centers are essentially eating the economy and crowding out a lot of other investment. Apple is looking for an experienced cellular modem systems engineer to help develop its next generation of cellular modems as the company transitions toward 6G. Here are the details. As spotted by MacRumors, Apple listed a new job opening yesterday for a 6G Cellular Modem Systems Engineer, with a base salary range of $175,000 to $308,500 per year, plus stock awards and other benefits. From the job listing: We’re looking for a Cellular Modem Systems Engineer to join our cellular systems engineering team as we define and build the next generation of cellular technology. This is a rare opportunity to shape the future of wireless communication at a company that ships at global scale as we transition towards 6G. In this role, you’ll bring an end-to-end view of wireless systems — spanning 3GPP standards, feature definition and planning, design, hardware and software architecture and partitioning — to deliver leading-edge performance and power optimizations and features that directly improve the user experience across Apple products. If you thrive at the intersection of deep technical theory and hands-on bring-up — and you’re excited about pushing beyond 5G into the 6G era — we want to hear from you. Apple says the candidate’s responsibilities will include defining features and requirements for next-generation cellular modems, designing algorithms to improve performance and power efficiency, and working with hardware and software teams to bring those technologies to market. The candidate should have a degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering, or a related field, along with at least 10 years of industry experience working with cellular technologies. Apple also requires a strong understanding of cellular communication standards and proficiency in MATLAB, C/C++, or Python. Interestingly, Apple also lists experience with generative AI and LLM-based tools “to accelerate engineering workflows” as a minimum qualification. Ideally, the candidate should also have a track record of published research or patents in wireless communications, among other preferred qualifications. For context, 6G is still years away and in the early stages of development, as companies and industry organizations work to define what it will look like. I really wonder why we never push existing technology to its limits before moving on to something that’s much crazier and that we will never achieve either.  I don’t recall 5G in practice being anywhere near 20Gbps. Not even 5Gbps. Heck, in most cases, it’s not even 2Gbps. And now we’re done with it and moving to 6G already? The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has outlined potential peak speeds of up to 200 Gbps, compared to 5G’s theoretical maximum of 20 Gbps, along with research targets for latency as low as 0.1 milliseconds. AI is also expected to play a much bigger role in 6G, helping networks automatically adjust to changing conditions, optimize signal quality, manage traffic, and reduce power consumption. The first official 6G technical specifications are expected to be finalized in late 2028, with commercial networks and compatible devices anticipated around 2030. Brad Gerstner, the investor and architect of Trump Accounts, is pushing to expand the investment accounts beyond children and make them available to every US citizen under 40. In an interview with CNBC on Wednesday, Gerstner said the change would require new legislation rather than a regulatory rule change. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts created under President Donald Trump’s tax-and-spending law. Right now, they are available to Americans under 18, while children born between 2025 and 2028 are eligible for a $1,000 federal seed contribution. When account holders turn 18, the accounts become traditional individual retirement accounts, or IRAs.  "Every year, 3.7 million kids age up into IRAs," Gerstner said. "Why not pull forward 20 years of IRAs? We can create all of those today, everybody under 40." Gerstner's idea would create the accounts for adults under 40 without necessarily requiring the government to make an upfront deposit. Instead, he said, it would give employers, philanthropists and companies a ready-made vehicle through which to contribute. That structure could allow companies or private citizens to contribute to accounts, he said, creating a "vessel" for the funding. On Monday, Elon Musk said he planned to give one share of SpaceX stock to every American child through Trump Accounts. Giving a share to the roughly 72 million children in the US would be worth around $11.5 billion, based on SpaceX's share price in Wednesday trading.  Other major donors, including Michael and Susan Dell, Ray Dalio, and SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell, have also backed the initiative. By Jill Goldsmith  Co-Business Editor  Netflix shares skidded 4% Wednesday after mixed-to-uninspiring quarterly earnings as Wall Streeters cut price targets on the stock.  	Analysts want proof of more muscular viewer engagement. They generally agree with the streamer’s co-CEOs that the key is culturally resonant, English-language series and movies that are home runs versus “the really solid doubles and triples this year,” as noted by co-CEO Ted Sarandos on an earnings call Tuesday. The biggest U.S. hits often scale globally, creating a tailwind for the platform.  	The quarterly results “did little to change the narrative,” Jessica Reif Ehrlich of BofA Securities, wrote in a client note. Calling Netflix a “battleground stock” due to debate over its path, she reiterated her “buy” rating but dropped her 12-month price outlook to $90 from $105. Nevertheless, she concluded, “While overhangs are likely to persist near term, Netflix has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to adapt, execute against shifting industry dynamics and compound shareholder value over time.”  	           			Watch on Deadline		       	Netflix’s slate for this fall and into next year looks far more promising than recent chatter and executive turnover would suggest, many analysts contend.  	“One breakout hit could shift sentiment to the positive,” says Morgan Stanley analyst Sean Diffley in a note to clients. “We think U.S. content slate fears are overblown,” agreed TD Cowen’s John Blackledge.  	Netflix’s results for the July-to-September quarter saw revenue in line, a beat on earnings, and slower advertising trickling into the current fourth quarter due to timing of ad product launches and integrations.   	On Wednesday, after the release of the quarterly financials, Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters convened a town hall meeting. Sources familiar with the town hall told Deadline the execs reiterated key messages from earnings and also memos related to last week’s layoffs of 1,000 workers, the company’s most extensive job cuts since 2022.   	           	More broadly, Alicia Reese of Wedbush Securities likes that “Netflix isn’t beholden to industry headwinds; it is in control,” she says. “Churn and pricing held up.”  	She went on to note that Netflix “is expanding its valuable live-events inventory, and it plans to preserve its content strategy rather than duking it out with YouTube on short-form. Importantly, management’s tone underscored its intent to shift toward a platform model as it broadens its licensing partnerships and add-on deals, in addition to reaccelerating its ad rollout.”  Netflix stock has drifted down toward a two-year low at around $65. That’s down by 25% year to date and over 40% in the past 52 weeks.  	Why exactly is a compound problem.  	First, Warner Bros. Netflix’s bid for the asset had investors questioning whether the streamer itself was questioning what would drive its next phase of growth as competition intensified. When Netflix lost Warner to Paramount, some got more scared – although mostly lingeringly in hindsight. At that moment, many investors were relieved to avoid a costly bidding war and liked the hefty breakup fee. Tesla has begun producing its long-awaited humanoid robot, Optimus, at its Fremont factory, the company said in its quarterly earnings report. "The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured," Tesla said, saying the current manufacturing process is "suitable for a commercial product." "There's still some things we need to tweak about the design, because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration," CEO Elon Musk said on Tesla's Q3 earnings call. "It can't, like, wear out after a month." Musk said the company will take at least a year to scale up Optimus production to 20,000 units a week in Fremont. He said he expects to begin delivering Optimus to customers at the end of next year. Musk tempered expectations about how quickly Tesla can scale up Optimus production because it is "such a radically new product." He said the early stages of production will be "somewhat bumpy" because "there's like 10,000 things that have to go right" to build the robot. One of the big challenges Musk outlined is building robot hands. Musk said Tesla is building an "Optimus Academy," where robots will practice tasks and generate data to improve the AI models that power them. The company also plans to install its next-generation AI5 chip in Optimus in April, which will give the robots more computing power and be a "big step change in intelligence," Musk said. The latest version of Optimus has not been unveiled. Musk said he expects to release a video of Optimus within one or two months. He previously said Tesla was keeping the robot under wraps to prevent competitors from copying its design. Tesla stopped producing the Model S and Model X at its Fremont, California, plant earlier this year to make room for an Optimus line designed to eventually produce a million robots a year. A second line under construction in Austin is planned to have an annual capacity of 10 million robots. Tesla is competing in a crowded humanoid market. Agility Robotics, which plans to go public, has deployed its Digit robot across nine customer facilities, while Figure AI has announced deployments in logistics and distribution centers this year. Sunday Robotics, 1X, and Weave Robotics are preparing to ship robots into homes this fall. President Donald Trump said that data center companies should pay local communities a "dividend" to make their projects "popular." In a Truth Social post early Wednesday, Trump urged companies to "MAKE DEALS," but did not provide details on how much money they should return to communities or individuals where data centers are being built. "I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck," he wrote in the post. There's been a growing backlash against data center construction across the US, with some saying the projects are noisy, raise electricity bills, and compromise the general quality of living.  Data centers are becoming an increasingly important issue in next month's midterm elections, and some politicians have shifted how they talk about the projects in recent months. Data Center Watch, a research project run by 10a Labs, found that in the first quarter of this year, at least 75 data center projects were delayed or canceled due to local opposition. Some companies have already started trying to placate unhappy locals with money or discounts. This summer, Elon Musk's SpaceX offered eligible Memphis residents a 50% discount on its Starlink internet service, tied to its growing AI build-out in the city. NorthPoint Development opted for a pure cash incentive and said it would pay every household in a Pennsylvania township $10,000 if it got permission to build a data center, the Wall Street Journal reported last month. In his Wednesday post, Trump also referenced one of his previous efforts: having tech companies cover their power costs when they build data centers to help keep local electricity prices flat. Several tech leaders agreed to do so in March, when they signed the "Ratepayer Protection Pledge," which mandates that companies provide or pay for the power generation and electricity needed for their AI projects, among other commitments. Tech > Services & Software > AI As delivery robots roll through cities like Chicago, they're fueling fears about unregulated surveillance in public spaces.  				Edited by Laura Michelle Davis  October 21, 2026, 7:30 pm ET Food delivery robots might not just be carrying burritos. They could be taking a measurement of your face.  Two proposed class action lawsuits in Chicago accuse Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics of collecting biometric information without consent and using it to train their artificial intelligence systems. The Cook County residents allege that the companies violated Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act, which requires companies to provide written notice of the types and purposes of data collection, obtain prior written consent, and maintain set retention and deletion schedules. Plaintiff Mitchell Breidinger said that even though he hadn’t chosen robot delivery for his DoorDash groceries, a Coco robot showed up at his home in September 2025. Breidinger said that while he was entering a pickup code, the robot’s cameras captured his face, head and hands and that lidar — a type of 3D imaging technology — measured the geometry of those body parts. Breidinger also alleged that a Coco remote operator watched the delivery on video and that the company didn’t notify him in writing of its intent to collect his biometric data or how long it would retain it. More from CNET The other plaintiff, Barry Schain, said he received three Serve Robotics deliveries with his Uber Eats orders even though he hadn’t selected robot delivery. The lawsuits seek statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation or $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation, plus other unspecified relief. Both companies have denied the claims, saying they don’t record the biometric data of customers or people who walk by the robots on the street. A Serve Robotics spokesperson said in a statement to CNET that its robots “use cameras and sensors to navigate the sidewalks of Chicago safely. Serve does not use that data to identify individuals, and our systems are not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles.” Coco Robotics didn’t respond to a request for comment, but a company spokesperson told the Associated Press that the company collects only navigational data “to make sidewalks safer for all users” and that it does “not share data from the beginning or end of delivery trips under our data sharing partnerships.” Robotic deliveries have expanded significantly since Starship Technologies’ inaugural package delivery nearly a decade ago. Starship said it surpassed 10 million deliveries globally by midyear. Coco Robotics now operates about 1,000 robots for deliveries in Chicago, Los Angeles, Washington, DC and Miami. Serve Robotics has more than 2,000 in Los Angeles, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth, Miami, Chicago and Alexandria, Virginia. Both companies primarily deliver food for DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub. According to most projections, global robotic delivery will expand rapidly over the next several years. One forecast estimates that the US market will grow from $252 million in 2025 to $3.1 billion by 2035. And it won’t just be food and groceries. Deliverables could include medicine, industrial parts and a wide variety of retail goods, and there could also be a rise in delivery by drone and boat. As fear and anger mount over technology increasingly encroaching on people’s everyday lives, delivery robots — which use AI, cameras and lidar to navigate sidewalks — are advancing rapidly. Just as the backlash against other AI surveillance tools and Flock Safety cameras has cropped up all across the US, there’s a growing pushback against potential privacy violations from delivery robots, which have been punched, kicked, tipped over and defaced, according to a recent story by The New York Times.  Privacy experts and digital rights activists also raise concerns that autonomous courier technology will eliminate delivery jobs and be used by the government or corporations to track people’s activities.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. Science The scent-sending technology could be used in online shopping, healhcare diagnoses and just for fun. October 21, 2026, 2:20 pm ET Want to celebrate your faraway friend with a sniff of fresh-baked birthday cake? Wake up a sleepy dorm daughter with the scent of coffee or oranges? It’s still a Jetsons-style dream for regular folks to send scents across the miles, but researchers at the Ohio State University are bringing us closer. They’ve developed a new system capable of detecting and transmitting smells across vast distances. That system, outlined in a study released Wednesday, includes two different devices. First, an AI-powered e-nose detects and analyzes an odor. Then, it sends that scent data to a receiver called a Scentronic, which recreates the smell for someone else. The team created a few versions of the Scentronic, including a wristband, a handheld model and a necklace. Each one is equipped with a five-channel scent distributor that uses a piezoelectric atomizer to spray the scents. (Piezoelectric refers to the use of pressure to create an electrical charge.) The entire device is powered by Wi-Fi and a cloud server that stores and transfers the scent data between devices. More from CNET The team used five scents: cake, beer, red wine, coffee and oranges. The e-nose detected one of those aromas, sent it to the Scentronic, and then the Scentronic reproduced the scent for the 16 people testing the system. Those people accurately identified all five scents. Chunyu Yang, a doctoral candidate at OSU and lead author of the Scentronic paper, told CNET in an email that these scents were deliberately chosen because they represented familiar but distinctive smells people encounter regularly in the real world.  Researchers suggest that this technology could be used in a variety of applications, including online shopping, to let people smell products before buying them. The technology could also be useful in healthcare diagnoses. A common symptom of COVID-19 is loss of smell, while migraines, pregnancy and other conditions can cause hyperosmia, a heightened sensitivity to smell. There’s also an element of sheer entertainment. “One exciting potential application is remote scent sharing,” said Yang. “For example, imagine enjoying a delicious meal and being able to share its aroma with a friend or family member who lives far away. This could add a whole new dimension to long-distance communication and make remote interactions more immersive.” The technology would operate in real time, allowing the e-nose to decipher a scent and transmit it to the Scentronic within moments. Once the e-nose analyzes a scent, the digital information can be stored in the cloud for repeated use. It can be transmitted to anyone with a compatible Scentronic device. The first time a scent was transmitted over data was in 2014 with a product called the oPhone. That device used scent cartridges called oChips and an iPhone app to release 10-second aromatic bursts, called oNotes. The various cartridges mixed together to create approximately 300,000 distinct smells, allowing people in Paris and New York to send smell-o-grams to one another.  Similar devices exist in the market, but they can’t analyze a smell. Users can choose only from a selection of predefined smells.  That’s where the Scentronic stands out. The system can both analyze smells and send them. “Scentronic uses a gas-sensor array combined with machine learning to recognize odors,” Yang said. “This approach allows us to develop a more compact sensing system that can be integrated with wearable devices.” Another company, Osmo AI, is also using AI to digitize smells. Osmo AI uses gas chromatography and mass spectrometry to map the scent at the molecular level and then synthesizes the scent in a clear liquid cartridge that can be dispersed to recreate aromas. Yang says that Osmo’s setup provides “detailed chemical information,” but that its equipment is much larger, whereas the Scentronic is designed for wearable use.    		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. South Sudan authorities say Sudan’s army launched a drone attack on a market, as MSF says it is treating 20 wounded people, some with severe burns. Save Share A drone attack on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by South Sudan and Sudan, has killed at least 153 people, according to a South Sudanese official. The Abyei administration’s caretaker minister of information on Tuesday blamed the attack, which took place a day earlier on Amiet Market, north of Abyei town, on Sudan’s military. Yohanna Akol Ngor said fires continued to burn at the site and that the death toll was likely to rise. He told the news agency Reuters that the “situation is terrible”, adding that some bodies had been burned to ashes. Blaming the Sudanese military for the attack, South Sudan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said drones hit several locations in the market. It said it has summoned Sudan’s ambassador and called for its northern neighbour to “refrain” from acts that endanger civilian lives and property. There was no immediate comment from Sudan’s armed forces. A senior Sudanese officer, who spoke anonymously to The Associated Press news agency, said the army struck fuel tankers coming from South Sudan that were headed to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). He added that those killed in the attack were RSF members and fuel smugglers, saying the military does not “target civilians”.      Unnamed diplomats told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market the RSF has used in the past to supply its fighters. There was no immediate comment on the attack from the RSF. In a statement on Tuesday, the United Nations secretary-general’s spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, condemned drone attacks near Amiet Market and Todach, saying dozens of civilians, including women and children, had been killed and many others injured. The statement did not identify who carried out the attacks. The UN said many people remained missing and the death toll was likely to rise as the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) continued verifying casualties. Medical charity Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said it was treating more than 20 wounded people, some with severe burns. The war between Sudan’s army and the RSF, which began in April 2023, has ignited a devastating humanitarian crisis in the country. South Sudan says it has not taken sides, but diplomats say Abyei has become a key route for RSF fuel supplies. Abyei is claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan, which became independent in 2011, and is jointly administered. The oil-rich region borders Sudan’s Kordofan area, which has become a major centre of fighting in the war.               Follow Al Jazeera English:

State Bank of India has identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information in a set of about 375,000 records available on the dark web, and it does not yet know where the data came from. The state-owned bank, India's largest, said in a stock-exchange filing dated October 21 that it "has experienced an incident involving the loss of certain data." The count is preliminary, and the bank has yet to establish whether the data is authentic, how far the exposure goes and what risk it poses to customers. The exposed information "reportedly included customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan/lead records and other related files," in the filing's words. A CIF identifier is the customer information file number, the bank's internal ID for each customer. The bank has not said whether the 3,897 records belong to 3,897 different people, or what the rest of the set contains. The 3,897 are roughly 1 in 100 of the records it examined. Account numbers, balances, passwords, one-time passcodes, card details and government identity numbers such as PAN or Aadhaar are not among the categories the filing lists. The risk in the listed categories is impersonation: a caller or message that uses a customer's name, mobile number, date of birth, address, branch, and internal ID to appear to come from the bank. The alert reached the bank on October 16 via its threat intelligence provider, CERT-In, India's national computer emergency response team, and the Defense Cyber Agency, the armed forces' cyber agency under the Ministry of Defense. The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and engaged an independent cybersecurity firm from CERT-In's panel of approved security auditors to assess what the filing calls "the alleged compromise." The incident has no material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, the filing says. That covers the bank's business, not its customers. The filing names no attacker, forum or dataset. The figure of about 375,000 matches a claim that the monitoring account CyberPulse56 flagged on X on October 16. The account said a threat actor using the name Siriusim claimed to have leaked customer documents and personal data linked to SBI: 375,000 rows in CSV format and 2,722 PDF documents, said to include personal information, loan applications and supporting documents, account-opening forms and addresses. The Free Press Journal examined the listing on BreachForums, a cybercrime forum used to trade stolen data, and found 4 sample records posted with the listing. The phone numbers in the samples were valid. The WhatsApp profile picture on one number matched the passport-size photograph on that person's KYC document, which the actor had also posted. That check covers 4 records and does not show that the whole set is genuine or where it came from. The samples were mostly loan-related and carried KYC fields, and they did not show whether the data belonged to SBI itself, one of its subsidiaries, or a third-party provider that handles banking applications. Nothing in the bank's filing ties its analysis to the listing, and the bank has not said whether the 2,722 PDF documents were part of what it examined. Whether any SBI system was breached is an open question. The filing leaves the source of the data to the investigation and gives no date for when the data first appeared. The filing does not mention whether affected customers have been or will be told. The bank's cyber security page, last updated in June, tells customers to report any cyber incident to report.phishing@sbi.co.in or the national cybercrime helpline, 1930. That is general advice, written before the incident. Bank of Baroda, another state-owned bank, told the exchanges on July 27 about a cyber-security incident in nearly the same words, including "the alleged compromise," after receiving "a communication from an anonymous source claiming access to certain data." That filing named a preliminary cause, "potential business email compromise." SBI's names none. Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Europe                                       hide caption  LONDON – Mike Coe never thought he would leave his dream home in rural Worcestershire, not far from Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare's birthplace. That was until Coe started researching the warming temperatures in the region. Coe had a job making videos for environmental activists, and ten years ago, when he spoke to his colleagues about the effects of climate change – and read the scientific papers himself – he started to get concerned.                  Mike Coe outside his "Passivhaus" on the Isle of Skye in Scotland.                                                           Mike Coe                                       hide caption  "I realized that it was likely to get very, very hot in the British Midlands, even during my lifetime," Coe, 69, told NPR. "I said… I think we need to move to Scotland." A decade later, now Coe and his partner Lizzie Stoodley live on the Isle of Skye off Scotland's west coast. There they have built a "Passivhaus" — a highly energy-efficient home — the second they have built. And they are glad they built their new home where they did. "Our decision to move seems to have been confirmed as being the right one, particularly this year," Coe told NPR. Friends who still live further south have told the couple that the weather was "unbelievably hot" and "incredibly uncomfortable" this summer, as the United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record, with five successive heat waves and widespread drought. But while southern regions warmed up, the weather on the Isle of Skye remained temperate. "I think there are quite a few more very hot summers I might escape by living here rather than remaining where we did," Coe said. Others are considering the same move. Susan Chinnery and her partner Steve Lewis, used to live near Milton Keynes, 50 miles north of London. But they began finding the summer months increasingly uncomfortable. "I hate the hot weather," Chinnery told NPR. "I remember 2022 when Steve and I… we were actually sleeping outside on the patio because it was just too hot to sleep indoors." Like many British homes, their Victorian-era house was designed to keep in the warmth, and doesn't have air conditioning.                  Susan Chinnery and Steve Lewis with their dogs Connie and Truffle on the island of Westray in Orkney.                                                           Susan Chinnery                                       hide caption  Lewis said that 2022 reminded him of the famously hot British summer of 1976, and he realised it was only going to get warmer. "I thought to myself, it's arrived," he told NPR. "This is the slow and inexorable decline into some new state." Last year, Chinnery and Lewis moved to Westray, one of the Orkney Islands off northern Scotland, largely because of rising temperatures. Melissa Terras also moved to Scotland, partly because of climate change. "When I mentioned climate change to people as one of the reasons why we were going to move north, people laughed," Terras told NPR. "They were like, 'What are you talking about?'" In 2017, Terras moved her family from Letchworth Garden City, a town 40 miles north of London, to Edinburgh. A professor at the University of Edinburgh, Terras chose a house "up a hill," mindful of rising sea levels. She says more people are now thinking as she did several years ago.                  Professor Melissa Terras, who moved north to Edinburgh partly influenced by climate change.                                                           Melissa Terras                                       hide caption  The trend is also emerging in the housing market. Real estate agents in the Scottish Highlands told NPR that more buyers are citing cooler summers as a factor in their home-buying decisions. Recent figures show that house prices in Scotland rose year over year, while they fell in southeastern England and Greater London. All over Europe, there are signs that climate is beginning to influence where many people are choosing to live, alongside factors including jobs, housing and the economy. Scientists say Europe is the world's fastest warming continent. Large areas of Europe saw scorching temperatures this summer, with widespread wildfires, and at least 35,000 excess deaths thought to have been linked to the heat. As climate change intensifies, countries around the world are grappling with more extreme impacts. At this year's U.N. General Assembly, Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, called recent flash floods in his country "a warning to the world," urging a "culture of preparedness" for future climate crises. Gaia Vince, a London-based journalist and author of Nomad Century, predicts climate change will drive hundreds of millions of people from hotter regions to more temperate areas this century. The U.K. has felt the effects, too. "We've had five almost consecutive heat waves this year alone, and our infrastructure is built for a completely different climate — everything is built for a climate which no longer exists," Vince told NPR. Britain will also see migration, Vince said, as people adapt their lifestyles and infrastructure. Wealthier individuals are already moving toward places such as Ireland and Scotland in search of a more livable climate, she said. Vince expects a similar trend in the United States, with the Great Lakes region and Alaska potentially attracting people from farther south. Some Americans are already making the move to Scotland. Jason Sorensen, a California native, moved with his wife, Christine, last year to Golspie in the Scottish Highlands.                   Jason Sorensen, who runs a YouTube channel called "The American Highlander".                                                           Jason Sorensen                                       hide caption  After experiencing wildfires in Los Angeles and hot summers while working in London, Sorensen said "something broke" inside him, and he decided he wanted to live somewhere cooler. "Between now and 2100, there really are only a few places that you could categorize as 'best of the worst' oases if things really go to hell," Sorensen told NPR. "Certain parts of Norway, the South Island of New Zealand, maybe southern Chile down near the Lake District, maybe certain parts of Alaska — and northern Scotland." Not so long ago, people who said they wanted to live in Scotland for the weather would have been laughed at. But for many living farther south, it seems the joke isn't quite so funny anymore. Anthropic's AI chatbot can draft a speech in seconds, but the company is now hiring a human writer — for $295,000 to $345,000 a year. Anthropic isn't looking for just anyone with a way with words. It wants someone with at least 8 years of experience who can quickly grasp technical concepts, help executives sharpen their thinking, and remain composed when news breaks. While some LinkedIn users reacted skeptically to the idea that the new hire's work would be used to train AI, with an Oregon-based author commenting that this is the job one would take if the "writer wanted to build their own gallows," communication pros say the Anthropic job offers clues about the enduring value of human creatives. Three professional writers and comms experts told Business Insider that young writers need to understand that the work starts long before the typing does, and that being good with words is only part of the job. “When speed becomes cheap, judgment carries a premium," Ann Handley, the chief content officer at MarketingProfs and author of “Everybody Writes,” told Business Insider. "I think we're seeing that value extended to the role of the writer.” The opening for an "Executive Communications Writer" comes as Anthropic’s own research shows how AI is reshaping its workforce. According to the company's report, junior workers accounted for 9% of hires in technical departments in June, down from 27% in early 2025. In May, Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao said that AI already writes 90% of the company's code, which shifted hiring needs in all office roles toward oversight, judgment, and strategy, away from the actual execution. Rao also added that the company may actually expand hiring because "there's no shortage of work to do." Handley said that successful corporate communicators need to become strategists for the company's leaders, rather than simply polish their language. "Good writers have always been strategic, in the sense that they have always made choices about what goes on the page, and what does not," Handley said. "The successful candidate isn't merely shaping language, but shaping thought leadership and how the team is presenting to the world," Handley added. "That means knowing which ideas are worth owning, which are worth exploring, and which are just plain dumb." Joseph Braue, the executive editor of Content Marketing Partners, told Business Insider that a large part of the job as a corporate writer is to challenge unsupported claims, avoid overpromising, and resist pressure to publish weak material. “The decisions I’ve regretted the most were times I didn’t push back enough on corporate or customer executives,” Braue said, adding that while many writers do collaborate with AI, they must control the narrative and ensure accuracy. The compensation for Anthropic's communication role is high compared to similar openings, and professional writers said that there are ways a new hire in such a role could prove they are worth the expense. By comparison, Amazon Web Services has a job opening for an Executive Communications Manager based in Seattle, offering between $126,700 and $171,400 in annual pay. Josh Bernoff, an author on business strategy and former executive with 20 years of experience, told Business Insider that a bigger pile of content isn’t proof of a writer’s value in a company, and that to get promoted, writers need to collect evidence of the impact of their writing. “If your job is to create market research reports, then you're only effective if people read those reports and say, 'here are the changes we're going to make on this product,'" Bernoff added. "Your job is to move people and think about how to do it before you start writing." Braue, who leads a content strategy team, said that writers looking to prove their value need to understand business language and check whether internal partners and key sales leaders are using their content. “Learn basic marketing analytics. Understand attribution, conversion, and how a pipeline works," Braue said. "Writers who speak revenue get promoted." For young graduates, the pros recommend practicing original thinking while learning to use AI deliberately, even if you don't intend to be a writer. Bernoff said he would urge all early-career workers to take writing classes and to practice using AI for research and efficiency while composing the words themselves. Bernoff, who conducts an annual survey on how writers use AI, said he found last year that writers commonly used AI as a thesaurus or search engine, but fewer than 10% used it to create content intended to be published as is. "If you're in a position to move your fellow students or people reading a school newspaper or your professors, then you're going to be taking the first step that's necessary to be able to move people in a corporate environment," Bernoff said. Ripple is giving institutions a way to bet on stocks, gold and oil over the weekend through its brokerage business, but HSBC says thin trading could limit how much money follows them in. Daragh Maher, head of digital assets research at HSBC, called the launch an “evolutionary, not revolutionary” step in a note to clients on Monday, a copy of which was shared with CoinDesk. “This is a rapidly growing market but not a very big one when compared to the Trad Fi markets they are tracking,” Maher wrote. “The stronger case for the product comes once there is sufficient depth for investors to express views and adjust risk when conventional markets are closed.” Ripple Prime, the brokerage formerly known as Hidden Road, now lets clients trade swaps tied to more than 100 markets, including shares, commodities and currencies. A swap is a contract that pays out according to price movements, letting a client take a position without buying the underlying asset. Trading firm Virtu is already using the service, Ripple said in its Oct. 15 announcement. The swaps track perpetual futures listed by Trade.xyz, a platform for stock and commodity contracts on Hyperliquid, a crypto derivatives exchange. Perpetuals have no expiry date and trade around the clock, letting a fund take a position on gold on Sunday while conventional markets are closed. Clients deal with Ripple Prime, which manages their collateral and risk across positions, and can use Ripple’s dollar-pegged RLUSD stablecoin to back their trades. Ripple had already connected its brokerage to Hyperliquid in February. But a fund looking to trade millions of dollars still needs someone willing to take the other side at an acceptable price, and Saturday showed how quickly weekend positions can unravel.  Nearly $52 million in leveraged chip-stock positions were forcibly closed in 10 minutes as selling spread from Binance to Hyperliquid. The shares themselves weren’t trading, leaving the contracts without fresh stock-market prices to follow, and exposing risks of participating in these newfound markets. Read More: Chip-stock bets lost $52 million in 10 minutes with Wall Street shut Meanwhile, HSBC expects early activity to lean toward firms trading price differences between markets. “Until that depth develops, though, activity is more likely to be concentrated among market makers, proprietary traders, and hedge funds pursuing basis trades than among institutions seeking strategic hedges,” Maher wrote. Basis trades try to profit from price gaps between related positions, such as a contract and the asset it tracks. The bank said Ripple’s success would depend on whether the service is cheaper, simpler and makes better use of clients’ collateral than existing brokers and venues. Ripple is already earning fees financing leveraged stock bets, as CoinDesk reported this month, expanding into a business long dominated by banks. The new swaps are offered through Ripple Prime’s British Virgin Islands license, with more jurisdictions planned. Ripple has named an early customer but hasn’t disclosed how much the service has traded. Like most of my colleagues who have basked in its greatness, I love the Hyundai Elantra N. It's a raucously livable sport compact that's still honest-to-god affordable, and I even like the way it looks. The angular, Lambo-lite styling has aged better than I thought it would, and the N's red exterior trim sets it apart from regular Elantras nicely. For some buyers, however, I can totally see how that aesthetic would be a turnoff, and to make the car more palatable for more people, Hyundai has unveiled the Elantra N Monochrome, a version of the hot sedan that looks a little classier. The bad news? It isn't coming to America... yet. Hyundai says the Elantra N Monochrome will launch only in Korea, Canada, and Australia at first, but the automaker does say it has "plans to expand to other global markets." U.S. availability, then, is still very much a possibility. Along with the deletion of the red bits, there are new black-painted forged wheels that look like they came off a way more expensive car, plus slightly tweaked styling for on the front and rear fascias, side skirts, and the brake calipers. It's available in two colors, Abyss Black Pearl and Performance Blue, although Hyundai says even those are "subject to market availability." The rear spoiler and mirror caps are made from carbon fiber if you opt for an additional "Upper Trim" option, and based on the set of pictures Hyundai published, it looks like the Monochrome will be available with either the manual or automatic transmission. The interior has some new Alcantara trim, and the steering wheel is wrapped in the stuff while also gaining black buttons that really do make it look snazzy, and less toy-like than the standard blue finish.  As a professional lover of cool cars, I don't dislike how the regular Elantra N looks. It's appropriately shouty for what it is, and on an academic level, I think the industry needs more of that energy. But putting my 30-something self into the shoes of somebody who actually might buy one, the red stripe-y aesthetic would be a bit off-putting in certain grown-up life scenarios. Thankfully, the Monochrome doesn't replace the regular N, but — like when Hyundai gave it a DCT — instead makes it more appealing and accessible to a wider pool of people. That said, this new addition comes at the tail end of this car's lifecycle, as the next-generation of Hyundai Elantra has been unveiled, and camouflaged prototypes of its inevitable N version have already been spied. Before that one takes over, the Hyundai Elantra N Monochrome will go on sale in its home market of Korea first in late October, and pricing is TBA. For reference, a regular Elantra N currently starts at $36,595 in America, including destination.
