One of the decisions that can determine whether a growing company scales smoothly or starts to strain has little to do with the product, the pitch or the funding round. It comes down to something far less exciting: Do you build the operational backbone of your business before you urgently need it, or do you wait until the cracks start to show and scramble to fix it? After more than 32 years in this industry, I have seen plenty of companies wait. The problem is that waiting can make the eventual fix more complicated and expensive. I am talking about the machinery that keeps a workforce running: payroll, benefits, compliance, hiring systems and the paperwork nobody dreams about when they start a company. Early on, a founder may be able to manage much of it personally, sometimes with little more than basic software and a spreadsheet. With a small team, you may know everyone’s name and understand every line of payroll. Then growth arrives, and the setup that worked for a handful of employees may no longer be enough. Founders naturally spend a lot of time planning for growth. They map out the product roadmap, sales targets, hiring needs and the next market to enter. What can get less attention is the point at which managing a growing workforce requires more formal systems and expertise. That point can arrive quickly. One day, you are approving time off via text or in a group chat. Later, you may have employees working in multiple states, each with potentially different registration, payroll tax, unemployment insurance, leave, wage-and-hour and other employment requirements. Managing people does not scale on goodwill alone. It needs structure, and companies have a choice about when to put that structure in place, which can help founders feel more confident in their growth plans. Recognizing that early infrastructure investments enable smooth scaling can help founders feel more confident in their growth plans, knowing they are proactively supporting their company’s future. Sharp, capable people can delay this for reasons that feel completely rational in the moment. The first is cost. Building infrastructure means spending money today for problems that may not be urgent yet, but delaying can lead to costly fixes later, risking your control over expenses and growth. The same willingness to do everything yourself that can help a company survive its earliest days can become difficult to sustain as the business grows. Delegating payroll and benefits responsibilities may feel like giving up control, but establishing trusted systems and hiring experienced professionals can help founders maintain oversight as they scale confidently. The third is visibility. Problems in sales or cash flow tend to demand immediate attention. Weaknesses in HR administration or compliance can be easy to overlook until they lead to a missed deadline, an incorrect filing, an employee issue, or another costly problem. By that point, you may no longer be making a deliberate decision about infrastructure. You are solving an urgent problem. Building early does not mean overbuilding. You are not creating a hundred-person HR department for a team of 20. You are putting the load-bearing pieces in place before the organization puts more weight on them. That can mean reliable payroll systems and processes that can accommodate employees in multiple jurisdictions. It can mean developing a competitive benefits program, since benefits can play an important role in recruiting and retaining employees. It means having access to people or systems that can help track applicable employment requirements as the company expands into new jurisdictions. And it means creating a hiring and onboarding process that managers can follow consistently without the founder having to oversee every step. You also have choices in how you get there. You can hire an operations or HR leader when the workload and complexity justify it. You can outsource specific functions such as payroll or benefits administration. Or you can work with a professional employer organization, or PEO, which can take on certain payroll, benefits, HR administration and employment-related responsibilities under the terms of its agreement with the client. Addressing those needs deliberately can help founders feel more prepared and in control, rather than reactive, and provide reassurance about managing growth effectively. I have watched strong companies lose time and momentum because their growth outpaced the systems supporting their workforce. Payroll tax mistakes or missed deposits can result in penalties and additional costs, including fines and legal issues. Expanding into another state without proper registration can lead to costly legal penalties, highlighting the risks of delaying infrastructure investments. Not every mistake becomes a crisis, and the consequences vary considerably depending on the circumstances. But correcting payroll, benefits, HR and compliance problems after they have accumulated is rarely where a growing company’s leadership wants to spend its time or resources. Eventually, growth exposes what the business failed to build along the way, so early planning can help founders avoid unexpected operational challenges and feel more at ease with their expansion process. There is no universal employee count at which a company suddenly needs a more sophisticated HR or operational structure. Instead, look for signs such as increased management time spent on onboarding, multi-state employment or compliance issues to determine when to act. Maybe you are still approving routine decisions that someone else could handle. You have started employing people in multiple states. Hiring and onboarding new employees are consuming more management time. Payroll, benefits or compliance questions increasingly require expertise you do not have internally. Or you have already had a close call with a filing deadline or an employment requirement you did not know applied to your business. Those are signs that the systems supporting your workforce deserve a closer look. The goal is not to build bureaucracy for its own sake. It is to put enough structure in place that adding employees, entering new markets, or accelerating growth does not create unnecessary operational risk. Scaling is not only about going faster. Presenting partners Share on social Julian Weisser Julian Weisser is the founder and CEO of Solo Founders and a cofounder of On Deck. I spent the last seven years helping ambitious people navigate the biggest barrier to starting successful companies: finding cofounders. Back then, cofounders were considered an essential ingredient for starting a startup. Building and selling were each full-time jobs, and there was simply too much for one person to do. Because of this, most successful companies from Facebook to Airbnb had cofounders. That led to the idea of two (or more) cofounders in a garage or dorm room becoming a core part of Silicon Valley romanticism. You'll notice that I wrote the prior paragraph in the past tense. That’s because things have changed. The amount of human hours required to build something useful and get it in front of customers has collapsed. With AI, it takes less time and money to get started than ever before. This is why, after automation, solo founding will be the default way to start startups. You don't need to take my word for it. Just look at the data: In the report I collaborated on with Carta, we discovered that the share of solo founders has nearly doubled between 2018 and 2026 to 39 percent of new startups. Startups will soon experience a flippening moment where solo founding goes from odd to ordinary. This won’t only reduce the barrier to starting a business—it’ll also change the default way that companies will fail. Harvard's Noam Wasserman found that 65 percent of high-potential startups die because of conflict between people, not the product or market. Taking cofounders out of the equation eliminates the main reason that startups die. But the more interesting topic of discussion is what happens after going solo becomes the default. If the barrier to starting great companies used to be finding or working with cofounders, what will hold back great solo founders from reaching their full potential? With solo as the default, the main reason startups die will be loneliness. The negative effects of loneliness occur when no one else is close enough to push back on a plan, notice when you're stuck, or simply encourage you to complete the last mile on an exhausting day. AI might be able to help you move faster, but it can’t fully replace another human to vent to or celebrate with. This creates a new problem to solve. The biggest way to increase the likelihood of solo success is not to add a cofounder of convenience—it's to surround yourself with resources and other solo founders so you can build "solo, together." In a world of increased automation, building a solo company will be more viable than ever, but that doesn’t mean you have to build totally alone. Note that the forecast is specifically for the inner displays of foldables and not the foldables themselves – there may be some delay between the time the display component is shipped and when the final product is shipped. According to the forecast, 29 million foldable displays will be shipped this year. As noted above, this might not translate 1:1 into the number of foldable phones shipped, but it’s clear that 2026 will be a good year for the form factor. Here’s another interesting stat – displays for wide foldables will make up 44% of the total display shipments this year. In other words, the newest form factor will make up almost half the market share (the other two form factors being the bigger, squarer book-style foldable and the smaller flip-style). This is in large part being driven by the popularity of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 and the Apple iPhone Duo. This is great news for Samsung Display, which builds the panels for both models – Omdia forecasts it will have a commanding 66% market share, while other display manufacturers (BOE, China Star, Tianma and Visionox) will see their shares shrink. According to the analysts, demand for foldables is weak in China right now. However, more Chinese are looking to get into the wide foldable market, so things will heat up. Huawei pioneered the form factor, but it seems that other makers needed some convincing that it will be successful. Finally, the vast majority of foldable displays manufactured this year will be the LTPO type – these are more expensive, but their fine-grained control over refresh rate makes them preferred over the LTPS kind. And since foldables are already quite expensive, you may as well equip them with the best. The Nordic market is hard for global brands to enter alone — independents hold 65% of properties, revenue-based leases push demand risk onto operators, and labor costs run above the eurozone average. Franchising is still underdeveloped, at 33% of rooms in Sweden, the strongest of the four markets. Demand is strong: Stockholm RevPAR rose 12% year over year between May and August 2026, Copenhagen hit 88.2% June occupancy with RevPAR up 13%, and Norway passed 40 million guest nights for the first time. For now it is a framework rather than a pipeline, and whether follow-on projects materialize depends on each deal clearing both companies' return thresholds.

By Liz Shackleton  pmc-media-editor-2024  	At this year’s Marché du Film at the Cannes film festival, it would be no exaggeration to say that Japanese content and creators were everywhere you turned.  	Designated ‘Country of Honour’ at the market, Japan was involved in a slew of panels, workshops and labs; played a prominent role in Cannes flagship programs, including Cannes Animation, Co-Production Day, and Producers Network; and also launched the Japan IP Market, a three-day initiative co-hosted by the Marché and Japan’s leading contents market TIFFCOM.  	The Marché decided to shine a spotlight on Japan in recognition of the strength of its content and intellectual property (IP), as well as recent efforts – by the Japanese government, local studios, and independent filmmakers and producers – to engage with the rest of the world. As Deadline noted at TIFFCOM two years ago, Japan was once reliant on its huge domestic market, but is now actively seeking co-production, collaboration and exports, focusing its efforts on North and South America, Europe, and the rest of Asia. In doing so, we built networks with international producers, distributors, and other industry professionals, driving strong momentum toward transforming the sector into an IP-driven industry that generates global revenue.  	           	“Following this, TIFFCOM will leverage the home-ground advantage of being hosted in Japan to promote Japanese IP alongside a diverse array of participants. For international attendees as well, we aim to make TIFFCOM a platform where they can connect directly with Japanese partners and unlock new business opportunities.”  	A key program within TIFFCOM is the Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake (TIPM), an initiative that the Cannes IP event was also based on, which brings together publishers and production companies holding rights to Japanese manga, audiovisual works, novels and games. This year, the number of participating IP holders has expanded from six to ten companies, including content giants such as Amuse Creative Studio, Kadokawa, Nippon Animation, Shochiku and Toei.  	TIPM organizes a series of one-on-one meetings between the rights holders and international producers, mostly from North America, Europe and the rest of Asia. In addition, eight of these companies will hold an open pitch event, with audiovisual support from Imagica Group, to present their flagship IP.  	“We co-organized the Japan IP Market in Cannes – the Cannes edition of TIPM – with the Marché du Film, and the event generated an exceptionally strong response,” explains TIFFCOM managing director Kaori Ikeda. “Thanks to this success, the Tokyo edition is seeing an increasing number of leading producers attending from Europe and Hollywood. We’re excited to offer everyone in Tokyo this premier opportunity to connect with high-quality Japanese IP.”  	Another key TIFFCOM track is the Tokyo Gap Financing Market (TGFM), which presents projects with Asian elements and at least 60% of their funding in place, that are seeking to complete their budgets through co-production, sales, distribution and other forms of investment.  	This year, the event has selected 24 projects including Vincci Cheuk’s Hong Kong-Japan co-production 38.83; Boo Junfeng’s multi-territory co-production Trinity; François-Marc Baillet’s animated feature Back To Tomioka; five projects selected through a partnership with Canada’s Frontières genre market, and three in partnership with Italy’s Cinecitta (see here for the full list of selected projects).  	In addition, TGFM talk sessions will introduce Japan’s various support schemes – including grants for international co-productions from Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs (Bunka-cho) – alongside funding from Canada and Brazil.  	Japanese producers have been co-producing with their East Asian neighbors in Taiwan and South Korea for quite some time but have recently been venturing further afield into Southeast Asia and Europe. “Two factors are driving this,” says Ikeda. “First, production volume is increasing across Asia as a whole, including Southeast Asia, and production capabilities are also rising.  	“Second, opportunities to build networks with one another at film festivals and markets across Asia are expanding. Platforms such as TGFM are facilitating mutual introductions, leading to an increasing number of co-production projects with Southeast Asia. Japan also recently joined the Asian Film Alliance Network (AFAN) with the Agency for Cultural Affairs as the representative member.”  	In Europe, co-productions between Japan and France have been the most common, but Ikeda observes that projects with Italy have also increased following the signing of an official Japan-Italy co-production treaty in 2024.  	           	Recent co-productions involving Japan include Sleep No More, from Indonesian filmmaker Edwin, which premiered at this year’s Berlinale; Ria, from the Philippines’ Arvin Belarmino, which won the Heart of Eurasia Award at Busan film festival, and Boo’s upcoming Trinity, which has around ten co-producers across Europe and Asia. Trinity, Ria and Janus Victoria’s Japan-Philippines co-production Diamonds In The Sand were all selected for various editions of TGFM.  	Meanwhile, TIFFCOM’s conference program will present around 20 sessions organized along thematic lines: intellectual property (IP), artificial intelligence (AI), Japanese TV, Asian Series & Films, market trends and co-production. Key sessions include an ‘Unlocking the Global Potential of Japanese IP’, with speakers from Credeus (Kokuho), Amazon MGM Studios and Netflix’s One Piece; an AI-themed keynote with AGBO’s Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes; and the annual session by the Association of Japanese Animations, presenting data on the anime industry.  	Leading Japanese broadcasters Nippon TV and TBS will host sessions on their international activities; an Anime Co-Production Conference will feature speakers including Ervin Han (The Violinist), and a “Beyond Country of Honour” session has speakers from Toho and K2 Pictures, along with TIFFCOM’s Shiina and Cannes Marché Head of Industry Programs Alexandra Zakharchenko.  	Last year’s TIFFCOM had more than 4,600 attendees from 46 countries and regions, an increase of 13% from the previous year, while international participation rose by 10%. As of two weeks before this year’s edition, Ikeda says that visitor registrations – mostly buyers and producers – were up about 10% on the same point last year.  	“East Asia continues to drive strong participation, led by Taiwan and South Korea, as well as a dedicated pavilion from Thailand,” Ikeda says. “Some companies from China, including streaming platforms, will also take part. And in a notable new trend, we are also seeing increasing participation from companies offering AI and data analytics solutions.”  	TIFFCOM is taking place October 28 to 30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho district, which is just a few train stops away from Tokyo International Film Festival’s main venues in Hibiya-Ginza. By Dade Hayes  Business Editor  Meta‘s third-quarter revenue beat Wall Street expectations, but earnings took a hit from the company’s settlement of a lawsuit filed on behalf of teenage social media users.  	Revenue for the July-to-September period set a new record at $64 billion, beating the consensus forecast of analysts of $63.3 billion. Earnings per share of $3.83 also beat estimates, but without the legal expenses they would have surged to $7.40.  	The settlement in the case, reached last August, provides for payments to the plaintiffs and others of up to about $18.59 billion. For the quarter, the company said its report of costs and expenses includes a $9.89 billion charge related to the agreement. CFO Susan Li said in the earnings release that the recently resolved suit may not be a one-off, saying the company is closely monitoring regulatory and legal developments. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the U.S.,” she said.  	Along with the financial results, the company said it is effecting a 2-for-1 stock split and creating a new set of Class C shares. The new stock will start trading in January 2027 and will be offered to existing shareholders. Proceeds from the new issue, which will not confer voting power on holders, will help fund the company’s aggressive spending on artificial intelligence. Li also said it could be used for employee compensation.  	After long struggling to assert the same dominance it has in social media in the booming field of AI, Meta has finally gained traction with the recent launch of the well-received virtual assistant Muse. If you are in the market for a new Android tablet, you cannot go wrong with the Galaxy Tab S10 FE+, with a deal bringing the 256GB model down to $599 on Amazon right now. Within touching distance of the lowest price the online retailer has listed for Samsung’s mid-tier tablet, if you’re looking for an upgrade and want the best balance of price and big-screen productivity Android can offer, this is the main contender.  Just like the recent deal on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, a deal like this on the Tab S10 FE+ probably would have arrived earlier in the year, but we all know RAMageddon is the culprit for the annoying price hikes every sector is contending with right now. Despite that, you can save a significant discount across Samsung’s lineup right now, and with flagship tablets starting well north of $1,000, getting the Tab S10 FE+ at $599 (down from its $819 MSRP) is a steal for what’s on offer.  For $599, you get a 13.1-inch 90Hz display, Exynos 1580 chip, IP68 water/dust resistance, an included S Pen in the box, 12GB of RAM, and expandable storage up to 1TB via microSD. That’s not a bad spec sheet, given how mediocre some Android tablets happen to be. It is a year old, but there has yet to be a follow-up “FE” version from Samsung and the Tab S11 starts at a much higher $899 for the 128GB variant. One of the key things to note is that this $599 deal applies to the Silver 256GB Wi-Fi model. So you’ll need to decide if that’s the colorway you have your heart set on. This is a heck of a lot of tablet for your money, especially when you consider how expensive high-end slates have become. The prices of brand-new tech are still ballooning due to memory component price hikes, but if you’re a patient buyer, it pays off because that 256GB onboard storage plus microSD support makes stocking up an easy way to beat the storage crunch. It’s more than enough space to download your favorite shows and movies for a long-haul flight. A $220 discount off the usual retail price of the Galaxy Tab S10 FE+ makes it a great deal for one of the most versatile and reliable Android tablets on the market. Apple and the Department of Justice have submitted a joint notice of impasse over how recent Apple’s documents must be to fall within the scope of discovery in their ongoing antitrust lawsuit. Here are the details. In March 2024, the Department of Justice, alongside 15 states and the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of illegally maintaining a monopoly in the smartphone market. In essence, they accuse Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations. Since then, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case. Interestingly, Apple and the DOJ have also reportedly been engaged in settlement talks behind the scenes. Back to the disputes, they have included how many Apple employees’ records should be searched, whether Apple must produce documents from outside the US, and Apple’s efforts to obtain records from 14 federal agencies, which the government continues to challenge. Amid these disputes, the discovery schedule has been extended several times, which brings us to today’s filing. In a joint notice filed today, Apple and the DOJ inform the court of “an impasse concerningthe cutoff date for Apple’s productions in response to all Requests for Production.” According to the DOJ, while the two sides initially agreed to a June 20, 2025 cutoff for the documents Apple would be required to produce, that date was based on the original discovery schedule, which has since been pushed back. In practical terms, the June 20, 2025 cutoff date was agreed upon with the expectation that fact discovery would be completed by July 31, 2026. However, that deadline has since been extended twice, and is now scheduled for late May 2027. Christofer Sundberg's already thinking about life beyond Liquid Swords Over the weekend, Swedish reports revealed that Samson studio Liquid Swords have gone bankrupt less than a year after releasing their debut crimebrawler. Founder and former Just Cause lead Christofer Sundberg subsequently confirmed that Liquid Swords are headed for closure. However, he was also quick to make clear that he won't be disappearing from game development, announcing plans to form a new studio that he's now offered a bit more insight on. "I’ll be back at it again soon and will share more about my plans for a new studio," Sundberg wrote as part of his LinkedIn post about Liquid Swords' impending closure. "It will be built with the current market in mind, with a solid foundation and business decisions that give the games and the people making them room to succeed. The lessons from Liquid Swords will be part of how I build it.I still love making games." While stressing that nothing's in place as of right now, the dev offered a more detailed picture of the thoughts he's had thus far in terms of how this new studio might approach development and avoid the same pitfalls as Liquid Swords in a chat with PC Gamer. "A small, experienced team, low running costs and a game we can afford to finish without needing every sales forecast to come true," is what Sundberg said he envisions, adding that having "room to make a wrong turn, fix it, and keep going without putting the whole company at risk" is key. Generative AI also factors into that equation, with the developer outlining that he sees it as being used "to help with prototyping, repetitive production tasks and testing". "We're not looking to replace roles with AI or treating it as a way to save money (or make money quickly), because AI is bloody expensive too," he expanded. "And cutting corners in game development has a habit of coming back to bite you in the ass." Sundberg went on to specify that he's "positive about these tools", but doesn't believe simply declaring you're 'AI-first' is a viable production plan or business strategy. "You need people who understand the work well enough to know when AI helps and when to switch it off," he added. "I'd like [people in the industry] to talk more openly about that." When myself and Julian played Samson earlier this year, I ran particularly badly afoul of the serious bugs which plagued the PC version early doors. Julian was luckier in that regard, and we both came to appreciate the distinct character offered by its debt-paying central loop, while acknowledging that both the bugs and the clear limitations the game had been built under meant that core idea didn't achieve its full potential. Here's hoping all of the developers who made it end up landing on their feet and aren't left with uncertain futures while their former boss happily goes about his next chapter. Contributing Writer, Infosecurity Magazine  	Almost 3000 ransomware attacks took place between July and September 2026 and the figure marked a significant increase when compared with the same period last year.  	According to an analysis by Nord Security, the 2894 ransomware attacks which took place during the quarter represents a 50% increase when compared with the same period last year.  	It also represents a slight increase when compared with the previous quarter of this year, as the July to September period saw an 8.6% rise in ransomware attacks when compared with April to June.  Published on October 21, the Nord Security report suggested that the significant rise in ransomware activity is a result of the impact of law enforcement takedowns on ransomware groups.  	Researchers suggested that the action against the likes of Lockbit, BlackCat and RansomHub helped to reduce ransomware activity during 2025.  	“Now, the market is stabilizing, and the numbers we see today are merely the first stepping stone in ransomware’s new era,” said Vakaris Noreika, VP of product research and development at Nord Security.  	During the reporting period, the two most prolific ransomware groups were The Gentlemen and Qilin. Of those ransomware incidents which could be attributed, The Gentlemen accounted for 383 ransomware attacks, while Qilin was not far behind with 363 recorded attacks.  	The third most active ransomware group during the period was Inc Ransom, which accounted for 110 attacks. Other groups which showed significant activity during the quarter with almost 100 ransomware attacks each include Krybit, Akira, Deadlock and Clop Leaks.  	But it is The Gentlemen and Qilin which remain by far the most active ransomware gangs. The two threat groups have traded places as the most common perpetrator of ransomware attacks throughout 2026. The Nord Security research suggested that a rivalry between the two groups is pushing them both on to develop new attack techniques for claiming more victims.  	“Based on underground forum activity we observed, The Gentlemen's founder appears to have previously run one of Qilin's top affiliate crews before a dispute over an unpaid cut, which he took to an underground forum and lost,” said Mantas Sabeckis, senior threat intelligence researcher at Nord Security.  	“His answer was to start a new group and lure his former colleagues away with a 90% payout, well above the usual 70% to 80%. This quarter, the breakaway The Gentlemen group edged past Qilin by 20 attacks.”  Read More: Why Ransomware Remains One of Cybersecurity’s Most Persistent and Costly Threats  	One of the techniques which has been deployed by both groups to remove the encryption element of the ransomware attacks. Rather than encrypting the data and holding it hostage that way, the attackers simply steal sensitive data from their victim and threaten to publish it unless they receive a ransom payment.  	“Stealing data is faster and simpler, so one group can hit many victims at once with far less effort. This shift is likely a big part of why attack volumes keep climbing,” said Sabeckis. “But that doesn’t mean encryption is going away,” he added.  	While ransomware groups continue to adapt and evolve, researchers noted that when it comes to the initial entry point for attacks, they have remained broadly the same. These include attackers exploiting compromised passwords, a lack of multi-factor authentication, on accounts and unpatched security vulnerabilities.  	“The names on the most prolific ransomware group list regularly change, but the way they get in doesn’t,” said Noreika. “What happens once attackers are inside may be shifting, but closing those familiar openings still removes a large share of the risk.”

Save Share Paris, France – Jagged shards of glass frame the hole kicked through the window of Hassan Rashdul’s mobile phone shop near Place de la Republique, the epicentre of looting and rioting that swept this part of Paris on Saturday. “I was crying,” Rashdul says, as he watches a CCTV livestream on his phone.     The glass countertop is shattered, the floor carpeted with broken glass. The display cases that were full of new and reconditioned mobile phones, iPads, and computers are empty. The walls where headphones, cables, phone cases and other accessories hung have been stripped bare. “It’s really terrible,” the 32-year-old Rashdul says. “It was very, very hard for us… It’s already hard for small business owners like us. We’re not operating to keep the business going, but just to survive, really.” Rashdul says he’s lost at least 70,000-euros ($78,600) worth of stock. His insurance won’t cover it, because loss from theft wasn’t included in his policy, though Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said the government will cover employee salaries of about 3,000 businesses across France affected by the rioting. There will also be a “dedicated support fund” to help businesses restock, the French government has announced. Lecornu has ordered more than 200 investigators to work on catching the perpetrators of the riots and looting. But the rioters are moving quickly: Some businesses say they found their stock being sold online within hours of being looted. “Stolen items from this weekend are being offered for sale on certain platforms,” digital minister Anne Le Henanff said on X. “We expect these platforms to remove the listings in question without delay.” She held a meeting with representatives of six platforms in the presence of Interior and Justice Ministry officials. According to the French commerce ministry, representatives of Vinted, Amazon, eBay, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok, as well as French online retail association Fevad, were invited. “They will also be required to cooperate closely with state authorities so that those reselling stolen goods can be prosecuted,” Le Henanff added. Around Rashdul’s shop, there are mini-markets, opticians, phone stores and cafes that bear testimony to the violence last weekend. Some are boarded up. Others, where there’s nothing left to steal, have been left open and exposed to the damp October weather by their owners. But amid his suffering, Rashdul spots a glimmer of hope. “There’s another side to it,” he says, “a positive – local customers, people from the neighbourhood.” These people have set up appeals on social media to secure help for shopkeepers, he says. “They really make you want to try again,” says Rashdul. “People are helping us to rebuild our shop, to get back to work and serve this neighbourhood once again.” But it will not be easy. It took Rashdul, who immigrated to France from Bangladesh, 10 years to build his business. He now calls himself a proud French citizen – respectful of the right to protest but also worried about the impact of violence on businesses like his, and on France as a whole. “Even though I want to rebuild, next Saturday they’ve announced another protest,” he says. “I know we’re in a democracy and there’s a right to protest, but if that ends up in more looting, then that’s hard on France and damaging for its international reputation.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together. Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (Â£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group. During Tesla's earnings call on Wednesday, Musk said he had nothing further to add about the prospect of a merger but quipped: "I feel like I'm tap-dancing through a minefield." Musk said that calling the merger a certainty would be "overstating" things. Tesla reported a slight drop in third quarter sales which came in at $28.05 billion compared with $28.1 billion at the same time last year. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle".  Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.  But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models. Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.  "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.  Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn. "I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said. China's voluntary GEO standards set rules for AI visibility metrics, vendor contracts, pricing, and manipulation. Here are five ideas Western SEOs can borrow. In a segment aired in March 2026, an industry insider sat in front of a hidden camera and invented a smart wristband that didn’t exist. Software generated a first batch of more than a dozen promotional articles, and he followed up with 11 more: expert reviews, industry rankings, and user evaluations. When reporters later asked AI models for smart wristband recommendations, at least two listed the fictional device among their top picks. That demonstration aired on China’s most-watched consumer protection broadcast. It took hours, not months. And nothing about the technique depended on the AI models being Chinese. Six months later, China’s advertising industry answered with something the Western search industry still doesn’t have: a five-part standard that defines what generative engine optimization (GEO) is, how its results should be measured, what a GEO contract may promise, and where optimization ends and manipulation begins. I’ve followed the Chinese search market for years, and this is the first time I’d recommend that Western SEOs read a Chinese industry standard closely. Not because it’s perfect, but because it answers questions our industry keeps arguing about without resolving. Here’s how it came about, what’s in it, and which ideas are worth borrowing. To understand why the industry moved this fast, you need to know what “3·15” means in China. Every year on March 15, World Consumer Rights Day, China Central Television (CCTV) airs a primetime gala built on undercover investigations into companies that cheat consumers. Past editions have exposed food safety violations, data harvesting apps, and fake reviews. Being named on the show can mean regulatory action, collapsing sales, and public apologies within days. In 2026, the show took aim at GEO. Reporters described vendors who promised clients that, for a fee, their products would appear frequently in mainstream AI answers, even when the content behind those answers was false advertising. The program called it “AI poisoning.” What followed moved quickly: The standard doesn’t say why it was written in so many words, but having watched how Chinese industries respond to 3·15 exposés, I see three motives. Pre-empting regulators. In China, a 3·15 segment is often followed by government rules. An industry that writes its own standard first gets to shape what “compliant” means before a regulator defines it more strictly. Saving the label. Legitimate agencies had spent two years selling “GEO” to brands. After primetime television linked the term to poisoning AI, they needed a clear public line between themselves and black-hat operators. As you’ll see below, the standard draws that line explicitly, and it protects legitimate PR and paid media as much as it restricts manipulation. Giving buyers a yardstick. Before the standard, brands had no shared way to compare GEO vendors, price their services, or verify results. Research firm iiMedia, as reported by Yicai, had flagged low standardization and a lack of unified metrics as the young industry’s core problems. None of these three problems is uniquely Chinese. Western SEOs face the same mix of overpromising vendors, incompatible AI visibility metrics, and an undefined line between optimization and manipulation. We just haven’t had the televised scandal yet. The series was issued by the China Association of Commercial Advertising (中国商务广告协会). It’s not to be confused with the separate China Advertising Association. The work was organized by the association’s AI Marketing Application Working Committee. All five parts are listed as current on China’s national group standards platform, which is operated by the China National Institute of Standardization. One point matters for how you read everything below: these are group standards, marked by the “T/” prefix in their codes. They are voluntary, written by industry participants, and not law. Their force comes from brands writing them into contracts and from regulators using them as a reference. The list of contributors is as interesting as the content. The platform names dozens of drafting organizations across the five parts. Mininglamp, a Hong Kong-listed marketing technology company, led the drafting of Part 3. Content and search platforms such as Zhihu, Sohu, Weibo’s operator, and 360 also took part. One name will stand out to Western readers: Publicis Group is listed as a drafter of Parts 1 and 5. A major Western agency network has already put its name to these principles in China. See also: Baidu Now Measures AI Citations: Here’s What SEOs Should (And Shouldn’t) Read Into It Much of the standard is written for the Chinese market. But five of its ideas work anywhere AI answers influence buying decisions. The problem every AI visibility tool faces is that generative engines don’t give the same answer twice. Part 3 says this directly: identical questions on the same device and model can produce different answers, so a single run proves very little. The standard’s answer is a minimum of 30 runs at the finest level you report on. Its own example: if you report per intent, per engine, per day, that means 30 runs per intent, per engine, every day. It backs this with a table of the standard deviation of measured visibility at different sample sizes, taken from a 2025 industry report by the China Association of Commercial Advertising’s AI Marketing Application Working Committee and Mininglamp Technology: Source: T/CAACCHINA 003—2026, Appendix A, citing the 2025 China GEO Industry Development Report. Figures as published. They are one standard deviation (roughly 68% confidence); a 95% range is about twice as wide. The published values don’t follow textbook binomial maths: the 20% and 80% columns should be identical, and the 60- and 100-run figures are tighter than theory predicts. Treat the direction as solid and the exact values as indicative. Read the 5-run row again. With only five runs, scores can only move in 20-point jumps, and a brand that truly appears in half of all answers will land at 20% or below roughly one report in five, with nothing actually changing. If your monthly AI visibility report rests on a handful of runs per prompt, its trend lines may be noise. Even the standard’s minimum isn’t precise: at 30 runs and 50% visibility, the 95% range is still about ±18 points. The standard also defines its core metrics with formulas, so two vendors measuring “visibility” are measuring the same thing: The standard also warns that share of visibility and average position depend heavily on how the category and question set are defined, so they shouldn’t serve as standalone contract KPIs. Two details are worth copying immediately. First, visibility rate is calculated only on category questions (“best electric car for families”), never on branded ones (“what do you think of Brand X”). Branded prompts almost always mention the brand, so mixing them in inflates the number. Second, if an AI model judges sentiment, the vendor must disclose which model, which prompts, and which rules it used, and keep human review in the loop. What to do: Ask your AI visibility tool or agency how many runs sit behind each number, and whether branded prompts are counted in visibility. If they can’t answer, treat their trend lines with caution. Part 5 bans vendors from promising effects beyond technical reality. It names two examples: “absolute control of model output” and “100% screen dominance.” It then goes a step further. Contracts must state the scope, timeline, deliverables, and acceptance criteria, and they must include a list of non-promisable items as a formal appendix. Western SEOs will recognize the problem. “We’ll get you recommended by ChatGPT” pitches are everywhere, and few of them say what’s outside the vendor’s control: model updates, retrieval changes, or the simple fact that no one controls what an LLM says. What to do: Before signing any GEO or AI visibility contract, ask the vendor for a written list of what they cannot promise. A serious vendor will have one. A vendor who resists the question has told you something useful. Part 3 describes five pricing models: project-based, by service units, performance-based, system-based (platform licenses or custom development), and hybrid. The hybrid rules are the most practical. In a hybrid deal, the fixed portion covering content production, corpus building, and monitoring should be at least 30% of the contract value. Performance fees are paid in tiers based on how far targets are met. The contract must also define which engines and settings are measured, the baseline, the targets, and how model updates or rule changes are handled. The logic is easy to follow if you remember the fake wristband. When a vendor earns nothing unless an AI answer changes, the cheapest way to change it is to flood the web with fabricated content. A guaranteed base fee for legitimate work removes some of that pressure. What to do: If you’re negotiating performance-based GEO pricing, agree on the measurement baseline and a plan for model updates before you agree on any bonus. This is the most transferable idea in the whole standard. The standard defines black-hat GEO through specific tactics: fake content, abnormal distribution, corpus poisoning, prompt injection attacks, fake traffic and reviews, forged sources, and maliciously disparaging competitors. Contracts must contain a clause prohibiting black-hat GEO, and vendors should refuse work aimed at misleading users or evading platform rules. Then comes the crucial carve-out. Legitimate advertising, PR, media placements, and influencer collaborations are explicitly not black-hat GEO, as long as the content is truthful and lawful and nothing is being manipulated. That sentence does a lot of work. It tells brands that earning coverage, publishing expert content, and working with creators remain fair ways to influence what AI engines learn. It locates the problem in deception and fabrication, not in the act of trying to be visible. The standard backs this with a “one-vote veto” in its vendor assessment. Any provider involved in black-hat GEO, corpus poisoning, or similar manipulation fails the evaluation outright, however strong its other scores. What to do: Write a definition of black-hat GEO into your agency agreements. The standard’s list of tactics, plus its PR carve-out, is a good starting draft. Part 5 recommends an error-correction mechanism in an annex. When content a vendor placed turns out to be wrong, or an AI engine misquotes it, the vendor should start corrections within 72 hours. That means updating the content it controls and helping the client update its website, knowledge bases, and other channels. The same annex calls for an emergency response. If a corpus error causes a major incident, such as a wrong price that moves a stock or triggers consumer complaints, related GEO activity should pause. Part 4 also sets stricter sourcing rules for sensitive industries such as healthcare and finance. There, only whitelisted sources count, and anonymous posts and unverified user content are ruled out. Western SEOs will recognize this as a cousin of Google’s “Your Money or Your Life” (YMYL) logic. What to do: Treat AI misinformation about your brand like any other reputation incident. Decide in advance who monitors AI answers, who fixes the source content, and how fast. See also: Brand Protection In AI Search: How To Audit And Defend Your Brand’s Identity A standard is only as good as the incentives of the people who wrote it. Before you adopt any of the ideas above, keep these limits in mind. It was written by the industry it regulates. The drafters are mostly GEO vendors, agencies, and marketing technology companies. Mininglamp led the drafting of Part 3, which covers pricing and measurement, and it co-authored the 2025 industry report with the committee that organized the work. That doesn’t make the content wrong, but rules written by sellers tend to protect the market as much as the buyer. The 30-run rule comes from inside the room. The standard cites a 2025 industry report by the same committee and Mininglamp as the basis for its sample-size table. The underlying principle is basic sampling statistics, so I’d expect independent tests to confirm the direction. Still, treat the exact numbers as a rule of thumb, not settled science. It’s voluntary. Nothing forces a vendor to follow a group standard. Its real power will come from brands making compliance a contract condition, and from regulators treating it as a benchmark of good practice. We’ll only know in a year or two whether either happens. Some of it is old SEO with new labels. Part 1’s four-layer framework (technical foundation, content quality, platform adaptation, brand mind share) maps closely to technical SEO, E-E-A-T, and brand positioning. The standard even cites Google’s E-E-A-T by name, with a note that it hasn’t been validated for generative engines. Western readers won’t find much new there, and that’s fine. The value lies in the measurement, contract, and compliance rules. It was built for a different ecosystem. The standard was written with DeepSeek, Doubao, Kimi, and other Chinese engines in mind, in a market where a state broadcaster’s exposé can trigger enforcement within days. The ideas transfer to ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and AI Overviews. The enforcement environment doesn’t. The fake wristband worked on Chinese AI models. I see no reason to believe the same technique would fail on Western ones. Retrieval-based answers everywhere reward volume, repetition, and sources that look authoritative. The difference is visibility. China had a primetime demonstration, a regulator’s response, and an industry that needed to repair its reputation fast. In the West, similar manipulation can happen quietly, and nobody has yet had a strong enough reason to write the rules down. If a Western version ever comes, who would write it? Industry associations are one candidate. The AI platforms are another, since they have the most to lose if users stop trusting answers. Notably, China’s effort included content platforms like Zhihu and Weibo, the kinds of sources AI engines draw from. Could Reddit, review platforms, and major publishers sit at a similar table? Or the push could come from buyers. Brands that collectively demand sample sizes, non-promise lists, and black-hat clauses in their contracts would create a standard in practice, without anyone publishing one. You don’t have to wait for any of that. Every idea in this article can go into your next measurement setup or agency contract: China needed a national TV scandal to get there. The rest of us can simply read their rulebook. The media landscape continues to shift as Netflix purges its executive class while Larry Ellison borrows big dollars to backstop his son’s Skydance media empire. Let’s start with Netflix. Netflix Cuts 1,000 Jobs, Including Key Executives Puck had the scoop before the layoffs happened, reporting on October 9 that Netflix was planning to cut about 5% of staff. Puck explained the likely reasoning: Netflix does restructurings periodically, though its last big public layoff was in 2022, amid the Great Netflix Correction and a period of slowing growth, and that reduction hit only about 150 employees, or about 2 percent of the workforce. The company’s share price has been under pressure since last year’s failed bid for Warner Bros. and amid slowing engagement growth on the platform. On the 14th, The Wall Street Journal reported that “the bulk of the cuts would be in the streaming giant’s product, tech, legal and human-resources teams:” Netflix, confronting flagging engagement, has tried a number of ways to get subscribers to spend more time on its platform, including adding live channels of programming, as well as bundling with other streaming services. It has added video podcasts and YouTube creators’ shows to its service, as well as live sports and events. While its rate of customer defections is by far the best in the industry at just over 2% in the U.S., according to Antenna, shares have fallen more than 40% over the past 12 months. Netflix isn’t alone among tech and entertainment companies making cuts. Disney and Amazon.com have both significantly reduced head count in the past several months.  CNBC reported that “Netflix’s biggest threat has been YouTube, but looming on the horizon is Skydance. The combined entity of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery has plans to integrate the two companies’ streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max.” The September 10 Nielsen US TV viewership numbers, which cover July, show why Netflix was feeling stressed, with YouTube way out in front and a combined Paramount/WBD poised to jump ahead, leaving Netflix in fifth place:  Matt Belloni of Puck has this chart about length of executive tenure at various media companies:  Some Very Big Names on the Chopping Block The biggest casualty of the layoffs was Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria. Variety obviously spoke to some sources kindly disposed to Bajaria: One word that came up in nearly a dozen conversations with industry players this afternoon about Bajaria’s pink-slipping: “scapegoat.” Netflix is obviously against the ropes again, after slowing user engagement on the service rattled Wall Street investors and layoffs came this week as a sacrifice to the share price. But Bajaria’s dismissal makes it clear, according to the numerous sources we spoke with, that content is once again going to take it on the chin. “People always blame the content,” said the source, “but you don’t lay off 1,000 people unless there’s a big problem with the business model.” Bajaria’s exit echoes similarly shocking removals in Netflix history — notably that of Cindy Holland, the company’s first content queen who oversaw flagship hits like “House of Cards,” “Stranger Things” and “The Crown.” Holland was ousted in 2020, when Sarandos combined English-language and international content under Bajaria (elevating the latter to the largest autonomous content job in the streamer’s history). Holland, one insider with knowledge of Netflix observed to Variety, built a business of boutique hits. Bajaria’s foresight was sharper, investing in local language productions and building up Netflix’s global presence (almost two dozen international offices were opened during Bajaria’s reign). She is also credited internally with pushing the streamer into live entertainment. Bajaria was on the “ground floor” of licensing deals with WWE and the NFL, which have proven significant draws for the ad-supported tier of Netflix subscribers, per the source. Her talent relations were on par with others at her level (Bajaria was ubiquitous at premieres and launches in film and TV, most recently at Sarandos’ side at the L.A. premiere of Ben Affleck’s “Animals”). “The problem isn’t engagement,” said yet another person with knowledge of Netflix. “It’s that the only lever to pull for revenue growth is raising the subscriber price. How’s that Bela’s problem? Where’s the CFO and the CEO?” Page Six has a more gossipy take: In a twist worthy of a Netflix drama, ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria only learned of her firing at 5p.m. on Wednesday before a VIP screening of “Nobody Wants This” — after the streamer had repeatedly reassured her that her job was secure… “She got f–ked — she got blindsided,” says a source with knowledge of the tick tock surrounding Bajaria’s ouster and the layoffs. The source said that, “she knew there were rumors,” she’d be let go, but was told in recent weeks that her job was safe. … “What was extra s–ty is that they made her go to these Town Halls and meetings of team leaders to be like, ‘This is a hard day,’ and to be all supportive and calm,” said one insider. “It’s like, just tell her to her face. They could have just fired her.” … “I’m a little perplexed,” said a top Hollywood agent. “Netflix is definitely looking for their next hit. They don’t have anything to replace ‘Stranger Things.’ They don’t have that big show that’s on deck. But how the f–k do you blame that on Bela? Other people have greenlight authority [too]. Bella was grabbing NFL rights and wrestling. I think Netflix is one of those weird new age digital corporations that’s like, ‘change is good.’ They are losing subscribers and the stock is down.” … “It’s like the last days of Babylon over here,” said a Netflix employee when asked about the mood inside the streamer’s Hollywood offices. “People are losing their minds over this. They’re either popping champagne or cowering in their offices.” During Bajaria’s four year run as its top programmer, Netflix effectively won the streaming wars. But more recently subscriber engagement on the platform plunged, and Netflix has been largely shut out of the awards race while the stock is down after its failed bid to acquire Warners. Some also questioned the purchase of Ben Affleck’s AI company for nearly $600 million. Bajaria came up through CBS and then Universal TV before landing at Netflix in 2016, and had a reputation for embracing more mass market content. She famously described her programming strategy as a “gourmet cheeseburger” in a New Yorker profile, and it was on her watch that Netflix expanded into live events, videocasting and game shows — genres Netflix co-founders Sarandos and Reed Hastings vowed they would never get into. Another high-profile casualty was Netflix Film Chairman Dan Lin. Deadline has the deets: Many were shocked when the ax swung last week and it missed Lin’s head, landing on his lieutenant co-head of film Doug Belgrad. It was seen that Belgrad was an extra layer at the top of Netflix’s film brass that could easily be let go, dollar-wise. Lin was expected to be safe until Rice took over officially on October 26. It was at that point in time the exec planned to assess the situation. What is all boils down to is this question: Netflix, what is it you exactly want? All of streaming has turned into basic cable as we get farther away from Covid, and Netflix looked to Lin in April 2024 post-Scott Stuber to ratchet down the quantity of features and at a lower cost. He arrived after being a producer at his own hub, Rideback. From 2008-2024, Lin produced movies that minted $6 billion at the global box office. Lin did exactly what Netflix asked, steering away from overpriced $200 million-plus, non-downstream features like Red Notice, The Irishman and The Electric State. However, he had a no-nonsense approach to filmmakers, and hand no problem reportedly pushing back on prestige content creators like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck. During the Lin regime, one source told us that relationships with filmmakers were fraying. Recently, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher opted not to renew his longtime exclusive contract with the streamer. That said, we’re also hearing there was never any bad blood between Fincher and Lin. During Lin’s run, Netflix saw its most viewed movie of all-time, Sony’s KPop Demon Hunters (325.1M global views). However, that was greenlit under the Stuber administration. For Lin and Belgrad, their bragging rights include War Machine ($80M production cost, 147M views), the animated movie Swapped (144.9M views, which broke into the streamer’s top 10 all-time list), The Rip ($100M production cost, 136M views), Happy Gilmore 2 (135.1M), Apex (129M), Thrash (100M views) and People We Meet on Vacation ($14M production cost, 77.1M). Still there wasn’t a consistent reseeding of the Top 10 Most Popular list like there was during the Stuber era. Also during the Lin regime, he acquired two-time Oscar winner Emila Pérez in addition to the streamer’s current awards contender, Cannes winner La Bola Negra. Again, Page Six has the fun stuff: Ben Affleck may have played a role in Dan Lin being shown the door at Netflix, sources say. … We’d previously reported that Affleck had soured on Lin,  an executive said to be making $12 million a year, over the release of the star’s latest film, “Animals” — and that Lin didn’t introduce the film at its premiere, and was only spotted on the red carpet. But sources say the issues were also over Netflix’s purchase of Affleck’s AI company, InterPositive. We hear that Lin, known for his penny-pinching, questioned the deal that Netflix made to buy Affleck’s outfit for $587 million. Then again, Lin wasn’t the only one inside Netflix who was skeptical of the eye-popping price — and many staffers there remain unsure if the tech is worth the bill. “Part of Dan’s appeal when he was hired was his dispassionate approach to budgets and cutting output, which is what [co-CEO Ted Sarandos] wanted at the time and liked about him. But fortunately that was all just a wacky mix-up and the “Musk” film has had its TikTok account restored. But there’s no mix-up about Larry Ellison’s borrowing to back his son David’s Skydance play. Buy Borrow Die, Larry The Wall Street Journal has an exclusive on Ellison’s use of a favored billionaire financial strategy: This summer, Larry Ellison was going to sell a big chunk of his stock in Oracle, the company he founded five decades ago. He wanted cash to help pay for his son David’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. Instead, in the run-up to the merger’s completion, Ellison added to a multibillion-dollar borrowing spree. He put up shares in Oracle, Tesla, SpaceX and Paramount as collateral, and increased his lending from five banks: Citigroup, HSBC, JPMorgan, UBS and BNP Paribas. In September, Oracle said Ellison scrapped a plan to sell roughly $7.5 billion worth of stock. The borrowing let Ellison keep his stock and avoid locking in taxable gains, and highlighted how billionaires often employ a strategy called “buy, borrow and die” to retain their wealth without selling assets. Regulatory filings in California, the details of which haven’t previously been reported, shed light on the number of shares Ellison leveraged for lines of credit, and the banks that offered it to him. Ellison is one of the biggest single borrowers in the world. Oracle in September separately said Ellison has 413 million shares worth around $58 billion pledged to back his personal indebtedness, without giving specifics. The stock he has pledged for borrowing rose from 346 million shares the last time Oracle disclosed it a year earlier. Forbes puts his total wealth at around $169 billion, largely based on his total 40% share of Oracle, the bulk of which isn’t linked to his borrowing. The California filings, made by banks taking liens over stock collateral, offer a glimpse at part of the increased borrowing as Ellison committed to backstop billions to get the Warner deal over the finish line. The banks that disclosed the amount of Oracle stock they had security over reported 87 million shares, up from around 30 million a year ago, according to the filings. It wasn’t clear exactly how much cash Ellison borrowed, but market researchers and private bankers said that loans backed by a very liquid stock such as Oracle would typically be for around half the market value at the time of the loan. That means 87 million shares, at their current price, could equal $5.7 billion to spend. The X account Marla Seraphine had some interesting commentary (plus a cool graphic):  The Ellison family’s financial position now connects several businesses that would otherwise have quite different economic characteristics. Suppose Oracle’s stock suffers a substantial decline. Like if the AI bubble bursts. That could reduce the value of Ellison’s pledged collateral, potentially prompting lenders to demand additional collateral or loan repayment, depending on the agreements. Meanwhile, Skydance could be experiencing its own operational difficulties and require additional capital. In that scenario, the financial backer expected to support the entertainment company could be facing pressure on his own borrowing arrangements at precisely the wrong moment. A financial safety net is most valuable when its resources remain available during a crisis. If the safety net depends heavily on a concentrated equity position that can fluctuate dramatically, its capacity is less predictable than the headline net-worth figure implies. And Oracle has its own enormous capital commitments associated with AI infrastructure. Recent reporting has raised concerns about the company’s borrowing and cash-flow demands. The businesses aren’t legally one balance sheet. But they are connected through Ellison’s personal finances and the market’s expectations of his willingness to provide support. I’ve previously invoked Kirk Kerkorian and MGM. Kerkorian understood that the value of a Hollywood studio could extend far beyond the films it produced. Libraries, real estate, brand names and corporate transactions could be financially valuable even when the underlying production business was troubled. The Ellison transaction has a different structure and very different ambitions. David Ellison has committed to producing more films, not abandoning production. But the financial question is similar: Can the economic value extracted from owning a Hollywood institution justify the capital required to acquire and maintain it? And there’s a more immediate question. Larry Ellison originally intended to sell Oracle stock to help finance the acquisition. Instead, he chose to borrow against it, preserving his holdings while assuming additional obligations. That is a decision premised, at least in part, on the continued value and liquidity of his investment portfolio. For a transaction of this magnitude, the distinction is significant. The Warner Bros. acquisition is not simply a bet on Hollywood’s future. It is also, indirectly, a bet on the continuing financial strength of Larry Ellison’s other investments. Ellison has concentrated so much media power, debt, and reliance on the AI data center boom that they all now lean against one another like a house of cards. Apple did not invent the foldable phone, and it certainly did not build the flexible display market from scratch. Reading time: 5 minutes Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra Apple recently unveiled its first foldable iPhone, but Samsung has been making foldable phones since 2019. With the iPhone Duo, Apple has brought some new thoughts and technologies to the segment, but the company is pretending it has invented foldable phones all by itself.  Just in time for the iPhone Duo's launch, Time magazine published an article glorifying Apple's first foldable phone and its new CEO John Ternus. The article tries to paint a pretty picture of a company engineering the future of mobile technology with foldable phones.   Reading through it, you would almost think Apple has singlehandedly invented the concept of a foldable smartphone.  Speaking about rival foldable phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Ternus claimed, “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy.”  The iPhone Duo is certainly a sleek device and brings some smart UI design innovations. But let us be real. That beautiful, foldable inner screen the Time article raved about is largely built on years of Samsung Display's innovations and the foundation Samsung's smartphone division laid over the past seven years.  Apple has historically relied on Samsung for OLED panels, and the foldable space is no exception. While Apple touts its custom polymer and nano-texture surface, without Samsung Display's years of research and manufacturing innovations in the flexible OLED space, the iPhone Duo simply would not exist, at least in its current form. .  There is a reason Apple is exclusively using Samsung Display's foldable OLED panel and not panels from LG Display or other Chinese brands.  Since September 2019, Samsung did all the heavy lifting to turn foldable phones from a niche concept into a mainstream reality. After the first Galaxy Fold's rocky start, Samsung did not retreat. It continued to push forward by improving the technology year after year, using early adopter feedback, and normalizing the form factor.  As we noted earlier, the immense hype surrounding the iPhone Duo only proves Samsung was right about foldables all along. By the time the Galaxy Z Fold 8 arrived in July, Samsung had already solved most of the hardest engineering problems in the foldable smartphone space.   In fact, the iPhone Duo reportedly had some production bottlenecks, which shows exactly why Samsung's years of manufacturing experience matters.  Ternus' “cheap and crappy” comment leaves out that the iPhone Duo is over 20% heavier and 15% thicker than the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which makes the latter an engineering marvel.   And Samsung achieved it by refining its foldables through multiple iterations over the years. Samsung also took the financial and reputational risks that Apple did not have to.  Let us look at the technologies Samsung brought to the foldable space first:  To be fair, Apple did not just copy Samsung's homework; it has indeed introduced some genuine improvements. Its decision to redesign iOS and move the app dock and other controls to the right side of the screen rather than leaving them at the bottom is a thoughtful software tweak that makes one-handed access easier.  It also made the foldable screen's crease almost invisible, albeit at the expense of the punch and vibrant color OLED panels are known for.  The iPhone Duo's curved corners might make the phone look more sophisticated, but it does not beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8's symmetry. Samsung's foldable is also substantially cheaper to buy and get repaired in most markets globally.  Apple taking an already mature technology, polishing the software, and marketing it as a revolutionary invention is a familiar playbook. The iPhone Duo will undoubtedly sell well, maybe even better than Samsung's foldables.   But let us give Samsung the credit where it is due. Apple did not invent the foldable phone, and it certainly did not build the flexible display market from scratch. It was Samsung that did most of the heavy lifting to popularize foldable phones.
