Save Share Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn. “This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wrote on X on Monday.     About 73 million children under 18 live in the US, according to US Census Bureau data. At Friday’s closing price of $146.03, the pledge would be worth about $10.7bn. President Donald Trump thanked Musk on his Truth Social platform, and claimed the shares would be given to children “through TRUMP ACCOUNTS”, the tax-friendly investment accounts for children created under his signature tax and spending law last year. The pledge comes two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections. Musk is the biggest known donor in the run-up to those elections, having given more than $276m to Republican groups since July. Musk has not said which children will qualify, when the shares will be handed over, or how. So how might the giveaway work, and who stands to gain? Here’s what you need to know: SpaceX, the world’s seventh-largest company, began trading on the Nasdaq in June at an initial public offering price of $135 per share. That price has been volatile. SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3 percent since peaking days after the listing. The shares are currently trading at around $146 a share. Every $1 move in the share price will change the gift’s value by about $73m. Musk owns 4.8 billion shares in SpaceX outright, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in August. Including unvested awards and stock options, his stake rises to about 6.4 billion shares, or 48.4 percent of the company. Giving away 73 million shares would reduce his outright holding by about 1.5 percent, barely affecting his control of the company. That’s because his voting power, which is currently about 82 percent because SpaceX has two classes of shares, would fall by only 0.1 percentage points, according to a Bloomberg Opinion calculation. It would be the largest single gift linked to Trump accounts so far.      Musk has not said. Trump said the shares would be held in Trump accounts, and Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, the tech investor behind the accounts, for “helping enable this”. Nearly 70 million Trump accounts have been opened, one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House. Investments held in Trump accounts can roll up with tax deferred until they are withdrawn when a child turns 18. Alternatively, they can be rolled into a tax-friendly IRA – a retirement account for adults – and continue with the tax-friendly status. Under Treasury rules published on September 30, donors can now gift individual company stock to children via the accounts. Families and friends making regular contributions to a child’s Trump account are limited to investing low-risk index funds. Families cannot refuse the shares on behalf of their children and generally cannot sell them for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner. Musk cannot sell or trade most of his SpaceX shares until June 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported. The accounts carry the president’s name, and Trump has tied himself closely to the gift. He thanked Musk on Truth Social, saying the pledge was “exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS”. The White House has presented the accounts as a signature achievement of Trump’s tax law, noting that “every single Democrat voted against” the legislation. The pledge also marks a public reconciliation. Musk and Trump fell out in 2025 over Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, a rift Trump later called a “little dispute”. Children will be gaining a share for free, but the gift could also save Musk money. Donors who give appreciated stock to charity avoid capital gains tax and can usually claim a deduction, the US broadcaster CNBC reported. As SpaceX’s founder, Musk paid very little for his shares, and selling $10.7bn of them could mean a tax bill of up to about $2.5bn. It is “a popular practice for particularly high-income taxpayers that would otherwise be paying a high rate”, Will McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, told the broadcaster in May. Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told Inc. magazine that millions of shareholders unable to sell would also have an interest in SpaceX’s success and in “minimising its regulatory burdens”. For Mitchell Downey, an economist at Stockholm University’s Institute for International Economic Studies who studies political influence in the US, the more striking part of the pledge is what he called “the horseshoe aspect of this” – the idea that right-wing and left-wing policies can curve around and meet. For decades, progressives have backed the concept of Child Development Accounts, investment accounts for every newborn designed to reduce inequality in wealth, he said. The idea was associated with groups such as the Democracy Collaborative but struggled to gain federal support. Now the idea may become more mainstream as a result of Musk’s gift and Trump accounts. “It always felt like it might be out of reach,” Downey said. “But I don’t see how Musk’s proposal would be possible without building some infrastructure like this.” The pledge comes just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the two houses of Congress. All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for re-election. Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result. Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections. Downey said he does not believe the pledge raises legal concerns. “Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.” But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach. Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television advertisements for a candidate. Downey said the precedent was “hard to assess”. Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”. He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US. Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”. Why Eggers' werewolf movie looks like it was dug up from 1922. 'Werwulf' Come with me on a journey of many horror references. In 1922, a Swedish-Danish silent film came out called Häxan. It was almost educational in nature, like a very early version of infotainment, and its subject was witches and witchcraft. It also happens to look terrifying. The same year, Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror came out, and its imagery was similarly beautiful and disturbing, with its brutalist and Gothic contrast.  Modern director Robert Eggers has already dabbled in the world of the undead with his take on Nosferatu. He's about to reenter that world with Werwulf, an upcoming gothic folk horror film based on the lycanthrope legend. It appears he's pushed his visual language even further into its silent film roots, with monochromatic frames that aren't fully black and white but sometimes a wash of yellow, blue, green, or gray.  Eggers and his longtime cinematographer, Jarin Blaschke, have spent five features replicating early cinema textures. Eggers told Esquire that they shot on film. But what is that look, and how did he achieve it? Here's what orthochromatic film is, how Eggers and Blaschke faked it before, and what's new on Werwulf. Aidan Paul took a stab at breaking it down, which is our inspiration today. Check out his video.   - YouTube  www.youtube.com   Orthochromatic film stock is a black-and-white stock that can't see red (only blue and green), so when photographed with it, unpainted faces read darker than they were, and any ruddiness made skin look dirty on screen (via Cosmetics and Skin).  That's why silent-era actors wore blue-toned greasepaint. Kodak made a more stable panchromatic stock commercially from 1923, cut its price to match ortho in 1926, and Hollywood switched quickly after that. "There'll be exaggerated gritty complexions giving actors a rugged, weathered, sickly appearance," Paul points out. "And that's why you see on the set of a lot of silent movies, you'll see that the actors are in blue and green makeup. A necessity to create natural, nice-looking contrast on the face when an option like natural red tones and lipstick or blush wouldn't be available." The Academy Museum (aka my favorite place on earth) has an installation to show how color filters and black and white film was used creatively on Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, in which Fredric March transforms practically on screen simply through makeup and light/filter changes. See on Instagram The Lighthouse was their first attempt. Blaschke shot Double-X black-and-white stock through a custom filter, because true ortho motion picture stock wasn't an option. He explained the filter in our 2019 interview. "The orthochromatic filter eliminates all red light to emulate film stocks that were predominantly used up until 1930. It makes The Lighthouse almost feel like an early ethnographic film. With the filter, things that have a lot of red in them, like skin tones, we'll record much darker. You see every pore and blood vessel." Blaschke paired 1930s and '40s Baltar lenses with custom filters that mimicked early-1900s ortho stock, which responded to ultraviolet, blue, and green but not red (via American Cinematographer). Blaschke told us:    'Häxan' Credit: Svensk Filmindustri Paul points out that The Lighthouse hid its ortho look inside black and white, while Werwulf puts it on display in color, much like Häxan did. If you haven't seen it, Häxan is a beautifully photographed film with crisp images and gorgeously rendered, modern-feeling tableaux.  In that era, film had to be tinted by hand, either using a dye technique on the film base or by hand-painting each frame. (Tinting was also used in the 1922 Nosferatu.) At the time, filmmakers used a loose color code. Archivists describe amber or yellow for daylight, red for fire and action, green or blue-green for the sea and mystery, and blue as the standard signal for night.  Eggers explained the cool, desaturated nights in Nosferatu as moonlight stripping most color from what the eye perceives, so he and Blaschke aimed for that near-monochrome look (via Fangoria). We're not saying that tinting is what was done here, but the look is very similar, and Paul points it out, too. But the truth is that for Werwulf, Eggers originally planned to shoot in black and white before switching to color, according to World of Reel. So he's starting on color stock either way. During prep, Blaschke told Phantasmag that this one would look grim and brutal. "The Northman was extremely clean—for 35mm anyway—with very fine grain. For Nosferatu, I let it be a high-speed film, and it's still a modern film stock, so it's not really that different. This next one, we're really going to try to give it some texture. And I've got some ideas. Early tests are very promising. It won't look like anything I've seen this decade, that's for sure." Cinelab, which processed the film, says it will publish more about its hybrid film-digital workflow on the project later. The process involves transferring digital video footage onto celluloid, developing the film, and scanning it back into a digital file to give it the film aesthetic. Werwulf is released in cinemas in December 2026. Let us know what you think of the look.

In 2026, nearly every major phone maker is eager to add “Pro Max” to their flagship lineups. Oppo is now joining this trend with its Find X10 Pro Max. Whether you see the naming as bold or just another industry move, one thing is hard to ignore. Even when manufacturers like Oppo pack their phones with leading-edge hardware and arguably superior imaging, they still face the ongoing challenge of measuring up to Apple’s influence at the top of the market. This device brings a massive 6.78-inch AMOLED display and debuts the industry’s first trio of 200-megapixel cameras. Its battery is also among the largest found in any mainstream smartphone. Oppo claims this phone stands out for both design and capability. After spending time with the Find X10 Pro Max, I set out to discover if this “Pro Max” truly lives up to its name or simply chases a label. Designer: OPPO        The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max carries forward some of the Find X9 Pro’s most recognizable design elements, including its signature square camera bump, now paired with an oval accent for the color sensor and LED. Oppo offers this flagship in two finishes. The Titanium Grey edition features a single sculpted piece of glass with contours that flow seamlessly into the camera area, softening the visual impact and giving the phone an understated, professional vibe. The grey itself is subtle, with hints of mauve appearing under certain lighting conditions. For this review, I received the Luna White edition, which channels inspiration from classic cameras and reimagines the look for a contemporary audience. The camera island sports a matte silver metallic finish with knurled detailing, highlighted by Hasselblad’s signature orange accent ring. The back showcases a subtle fabric-inspired pattern, with Oppo and Hasselblad branding on the side. While both colors exude sophistication, those who prefer darker tones or bolder shades may find themselves wishing for greater variety in the color lineup.         Despite its impressive size and powerful hardware, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max manages to feel thoughtfully balanced in hand. My review unit is the global version, which comes with a substantial 8000mAh battery and weighs 235 grams (about 8.29 ounces) in Titanium Grey or 233 grams (about 8.22 ounces) in Luna White. The EU version features a slightly smaller 7150mAh battery and is a bit lighter at 228 grams (about 8.04 ounces) for Titanium Grey and 226 grams (about 7.97 ounces) for Luna White. Measuring 161.32 x 76.57 x 8.40 mm, or approximately 6.35 x 3.02 x 0.33 inches, this phone clearly fits into the large flagship category, yet its slim profile keeps it manageable. The weight of the Find X10 Pro Max is certainly noticeable each time you pick it up, although the distribution helps maintain comfort during longer use. Both color options have a matte back and frame that do an excellent job resisting fingerprints and smudges, while also offering a velvety texture that is genuinely pleasant to touch. The device maintains a clean look throughout the day and feels luxurious with every interaction. The edges are only slightly curved, almost flat and straighter than on many other flagships, so they do not dig into your hand but may affect comfort depending on how you hold the phone over time.        The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max delivers the kind of fluid, responsive experience you expect from a flagship. Powered by the Dimensity 9600 Pro, the phone handles daily tasks, multitasking, and demanding apps without any noticeable lag or slowdowns. ColorOS 17 brings a polished feel with more refinement than revolution, ensuring that every interaction is smooth and intuitive. Everything from app launches to switching between tasks happens with impressive speed and reliability. The large 6.78-inch LTPO AMOLED display stands out with a sharp 2772 × 1272 resolution and vibrant colors, thanks to BT.2020 coverage and 10-bit color support. Bezels measure just 1.15mm and are perfectly symmetrical, which makes the screen feel even more expansive. With up to 3,600 nits peak HDR brightness, visibility outdoors is excellent. The adaptive refresh rate ranges from 1 to 120Hz for smooth scrolling, while 144Hz is available in select gaming scenarios for extra fluidity. The speakers provide plenty of volume, though sound quality does not really stand out. Hasselblad Hi-Res (50MP) mode, main camera, 1x Main Camera, 1x Over the past few years, smartphone cameras have leaned heavily on computational processing to overcome the limitations of small lenses. Sometimes the results are impressive, but too much digital magic can leave photos looking punchy or even artificial. With the Find X10 Pro Max, Oppo takes a different route by aiming for images that genuinely match what you saw in real life. The brand continues its collaboration with Hasselblad to fine-tune color science, and this generation introduces the LUMO True Image Engine, which keeps colors believable and resists the urge to overdo sharpening or saturation. Oppo debuts the industry’s first triple 200-megapixel camera system in the Find X10 Pro Max. You get a 200MP main camera (Samsung ISOCELL HPC, 1/1.3″, f/1.5 with OIS), a 200MP ultra-wide (Samsung ISOCELL HP5, 1/1.56″, f/2.2 with autofocus), and a 200MP periscope telephoto (Samsung ISOCELL HP5, 1/1.56″, f/2.1 with OIS). Flip the phone around and you’ll find a 50MP front camera (Samsung ISOCELL JN5, 1/2.75”, autofocus, 100° FOV). Ultrawide, 0.5x Telephoto, 3x Telephoto, 6x The headline megapixel count is only part of the story. The main sensor leverages DeepPix technology, redesigning each pixel to improve light-gathering efficiency and preserve detail even in challenging conditions. It delivers up to 17 stops of dynamic range for images full of nuance from shadow to highlight. Daylight photos are crisp and vibrant, and low-light shots stay clear and accurate. Most flagships treat ultra-wide cameras as a weak spot, but Oppo breaks that trend by using the same large sensor in both its ultra-wide and telephoto modules as in the main camera. The ultra-wide’s 13mm-equivalent focal length provides an expansive 124-degree field of view and captures sharp images across the frame. There is still some noticeable lens distortion at the edges, which is common for lenses this wide, but overall image quality remains impressively crisp. Color consistency is another area where Oppo truly excels. Tones stay remarkably uniform across all three lenses, so your shots always look cohesive. Ultrawide, 0.5x Main Camera, 1x Main Camera, 1x Telephoto, 3x Personally, I love shooting with the telephoto camera on the X10 Pro Max. It is genuinely a treat for anyone who enjoys zoom photography. Hasselblad Master mode is another highlight because it delivers a more natural, less processed look that gives images a classic photographic character rather than an overdone “smartphone” feel. For those who want total control, Pro mode within Hasselblad Master mode allows for granular manual adjustments. For users seeking more flexibility, Oppo offers a Hasselblad Teleconverter Kit in Luna White that includes a MagSafe-compatible case, lens adapter plate, teleconverter lens, lens bracket, shoulder strap, and pouch, all in silver or white with orange accents to match the Luna White phone version. While I love how visually unified the kit appears, attaching the lens adapter plate blocks both the main and ultra-wide lenses at once, just like on the Find X9 Pro teleconverter. This can limit your photo options when using the kit.  Telephoto Converter, 20x Telephoto Converter, 40x Oppo’s camera app supplies a nice set of filters. The selection is not as broad as Vivo’s catalog but still offers plenty of creative and customizable choices. Each filter lets you tweak tonality, saturation, and intensity to match your style preferences. My main gripe is with how OPPO lays out these filters: instead of small thumbnails along the bottom edge like most brands use, you only see one filter preview filling the UI at a time. This makes it tougher to quickly browse options and can slow down creative experimentation. Filter UI Open Gate Mode Video performance keeps pace with stills. All three rear cameras support up to 8K at 30fps, 4K at 60fps, and even 4K at 120fps for dramatic slow motion. The front camera supports up to 4K at 60fps for sharp selfies and vlogs. If you apply creative filters during recording, output is capped at 1080p at 30fps. Open Gate recording is available on all rear cameras as well, so creators can leverage every pixel for flexible cropping in post-production. My global review unit features a massive 8000mAh battery, while the EU version is equipped with a still-impressive 7150mAh cell. Both models support fast charging, with 80W SUPERVOOC wired charging making it easy to top up quickly and 50W AIRVOOC wireless charging for added convenience. Battery life is outstanding. It easily lasts more than a full day of heavy use and can reach two days with moderate usage. Main Camera, 1x, Night Oppo positions the Find X10 Pro Max as a durable and future-proof flagship, but most of its claims align with what’s now expected at the high end. The phone comes with IP66, IP68, and IP69 ratings, so it stands up well to dust and water in a wide range of scenarios. Both the front and back are protected by OPPO Crystal Guard Glass, co-developed with Corning, promising solid scratch and drop resistance. SGS Five-Star Drop Resistance Certification adds further reassurance, though these certifications have become standard for premium smartphones.   Oppo also states that the battery should retain over 80% of its original capacity after five years of typical use, which is consistent with leading brands but does not set a new bar. The promise of five years of major Android OS updates and six years of security patches is definitely good news for long-term owners and matches current flagship expectations. That said, it would be great to see Oppo take additional steps in sustainability, such as using more recycled materials in construction and offering easier repair options, to truly stand out in this space.  Official pricing was unavailable at the time of writing this review, but the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is rumored to launch at €1,799 (about $1,900) for the 16GB+512GB EU version. This firmly places it among the highest-priced flagships on the market and marks a clear jump from last year’s Find X9 Pro (€1,299, or around $1,370) and even the Find X9 Ultra (€1,699, or about $1,790). A significant part of this price hike likely comes from soaring RAM and storage costs, driven by increased demand from the AI boom and broader tech trends. If these figures are correct, Oppo will face an uphill battle. Even with top-of-the-line hardware and some of the best mobile imaging features available, nearly two thousand dollars is a serious investment, especially as many consumers are feeling economic pressure. The EU version of the Find X10 Pro Max is even more expensive than both the iPhone 18 Pro Max with 512GB of storage and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra 512GB model in the U.S. For Oppo to justify this price point, buyers will need to be truly convinced by its unique camera system and design philosophy. Otherwise, many may find more value in established alternatives from Apple or Samsung.   The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max stands out as a well-balanced flagship that gets almost everything right and, at times, feels nearly flawless. What really sets it apart is its excellent mobile photography, from the industry-first triple 200-megapixel camera system to the natural color science developed in partnership with Hasselblad. Everyday performance is smooth, build quality is unquestionably premium, and battery life ranks among the best available in any flagship. On the flip side, the high price tag puts the Find X10 Pro Max in direct competition with industry giants. While it delivers top-tier hardware and leading imaging capability, buyers must be willing to stretch both their expectations and their budgets. For those who put a premium on cutting-edge camera features and want an alternative to Apple or Samsung, Oppo’s latest is a compelling choice. For everyone else, especially those mindful of budget, there are several strong alternatives on the market that may offer a more accessible fit. Families say they are struggling to provide nutritious meals for their children as commercial supplies are disrupted. Save Share Gaza City, Gaza Strip – It has been months since Huda Abu Leila had to resort to serving only tea and bread to her five daughters for breakfast. But this week, that’s what the 30-year-old has had to do, after Israel restricted the entry of goods into Gaza earlier this month. After living through three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the accompanying blockade that often leaves markets partly empty and goods unaffordable, Huda is used to struggling to provide her children – aged between 18 months and 10 years – with a balanced and nutritious diet. But the current situation, with shortages of commercial goods, rising food prices, and cuts to humanitarian assistance, has made it ever harder for her to put enough food on the table. “We were affected immediately. We couldn’t find eggs or milk, and we don’t have the money to stock up on food,” Huda said. She lives with her daughters in a tent in western Gaza City. Her husband was injured during the war and can no longer work, while she earns a little money by baking bread for other people. Some days, the family eats canned beans with duqqa – a local spice blend – or za’atar. On days when food is not as readily available, like this week, they dip bread in tea. What worries her most is how the worsening situation will affect her children’s health, particularly as she is already struggling to provide them with enough nutritious food. Israel halted commercial shipments into Gaza on October 14, disrupting supplies of food and other essential goods as families already struggling with high prices faced further shortages. The suspension came amid a dispute over a demand for merchants to pay 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck to bring goods into the enclave. On October 19, Israel announced that commercial shipments would gradually resume. The Israeli military body responsible for coordinating aid and commercial access to Gaza, COGAT, said merchants had reported that Hamas had withdrawn the demand. Hamas described the payment as a voluntary contribution to a fund supporting people affected by the war. The disruption comes as humanitarian assistance is also reduced. On October 19, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut food assistance in Gaza. The programme reduced the number of people it supports from 1.6 million in September to 1.1 million in October. It has also halved food rations, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, alongside a smaller bag of wheat flour. The number of hot meals WFP provides daily has been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000. WFP said about 1.4 million people in Gaza, approximately two-thirds of the population, were facing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. Famine was declared in Gaza City in August 2025. The UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification said in December of the same year that it had receded after the beginning of the Gaza ceasefire two months earlier. For Huda, the crisis means she can no longer afford many of the foods her daughters need for a balanced and nutritious diet. Eggs have become too expensive. A shopkeeper recently quoted her 60 shekels ($19.40) for a tray. She also said some shops appeared to be holding back stock. Fresh vegetables have also become difficult to afford. When she goes to the market, which she usually does about once a week, she buys only small quantities. “Onions cost about 10 shekels [$3.25] per kilogramme, while tomatoes cost between 10 and 15 shekels per kilogramme [$3.25 and $4.85],” she said. The vast majority of Gaza’s population is unemployed as a result of Israel’s war and its restrictions on allowing the territory to rebuild its infrastructure and economy. The lack of food is starting to have an impact on Huda’s children. She says that they are struggling to concentrate, and often become dizzy and exhausted. The health of her eldest daughter, Salma, has become so poor that she is receiving follow-up care at al-Rantisi Hospital in Gaza, where a doctor advised Huda to improve her daughter’s diet. “We have been through so much hardship over the past three years,” she said. “I worry that my daughters will get sick if I cannot provide them with enough nutritious food.” For Raeda Soboh, 40, the struggle to feed her nine-member family means her children have gone months without some of the foods they need to stay healthy. The displaced mother, originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza but now living in Gaza City, said her family had long depended on community kitchens, known locally as tekkiya, even before the latest disruption to commercial supplies. “When a kitchen has food, we eat from it,” she said. Her children usually have tea for breakfast and a meal from a community kitchen for lunch. In the evening, they sometimes eat falafel, rice, lentils or pasta. But milk, meat, eggs and cheese have been absent from their diet for about eight months, she said. She last bought vegetables about a month ago. “I don’t buy good-quality things. I buy only what we need and what we can manage to pay for,” Soboh said. Her experience reflects wider concerns about children’s nutrition across Gaza. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 2,800 children were admitted for malnutrition treatment in September, including more than 360 with severe acute malnutrition. About 3,000 children aged between six months and five years continued to be admitted for malnutrition treatment each month, OCHA said in a report published on October 19. A UNICEF-supported nutrition survey published in August also found that 12.2 percent of children under five in areas accessible to researchers were affected by stunting, a sign of impaired growth associated with prolonged nutritional and health problems. Dr Mohamed B Alraee, a paediatrician and nutrition specialist in Gaza City, warned that prolonged restrictions on food supplies entering Gaza could lead to a further increase in child malnutrition, with children already missing the balanced meals they need to grow and recover. Despite improvements after earlier periods of famine, hospitals continue to receive children with moderate and severe malnutrition, he said. Cases are not limited to children under five, with older children, including those aged five to 17, also affected. Alraee said some children were suffering from severe malnutrition accompanied by swelling in the legs, a condition associated with serious protein deficiency. He linked these cases to families surviving on a single meal dominated by carbohydrates without enough protein, because they cannot afford more nutritious food. “Even when the crossings were open and food was entering, we were still seeing these cases. Children do not recover from malnutrition in a month or two. Some cases need three to six months to recover,” he said. “If the situation continues like this, we expect to see more cases of malnutrition.” For Raeda, the consequences are already visible in her children’s daily lives. She said they had become weak and easily exhausted, leaving her worried about what months of inadequate food could mean for their health. “They seem to spend the whole day sleeping. When I ask one of them to carry a water container, he might manage it once but cannot do it a second time,” she said. “I feel sorry for him and ask myself: is he getting proper nutrition? Is he eating like other children?” The family has no reliable source of income, Raeda said. She also said the area where they live is not recognised as an official camp, leaving them without the same aid vouchers and hygiene supplies received by some other camps. Like many parents in Gaza, she is left trying to meet their basic needs with whatever food she can find and afford. “I hope someone will help us and stand with us in these difficult circumstances,” Raeda said. “I hope the war ends, the situation improves and the crossings open, so prices can come down.”               Follow Al Jazeera English:

Over the past couple of weeks, I've been investigating an apparent wave of undeserved bans across the Forza Horizon community on Xbox, particularly in Japan. Japan has a strong and unique car culture, and Playground Games acknowledged that Japan has been the most-requested setting for their popular Forza Horizon franchise. Forza Horizon is now in its 6th installment, which is currently available exclusively on Xbox Series X|S and PC. Indeed, general Xbox adoption in Japan has generally been anemic at best. Microsoft has historically struggled to compete against PlayStation and Nintendo in the region for a variety of reasons. Microsoft's U.S.-centricity has long prevented it from achieving reasonable penetration outside of its traditional English-first markets. Forza Horizon set in Japan should've been a chance to change Xbox's fortunes in at least one region, but the RAMpocalypse has put a stop to that. But even beyond simply maintaining Xbox Series X|S stock levels, Microsoft has drawn the ire of some Japanese Forza Horizon players, who have once again put a spotlight on its haphazard community management systems.      Japanese "Itasha (痛車)" user-generated liveries seem to be at the center of the ban waves Playground Games has been handing out for Forza Horizon 6 players. Itasha is a car subculture, literally meaning "painful car," ironically celebrating overly flashy or "cringy" car liveries. The culture represents a nexus of sorts between car culture and anime culture, going all the way back to the 1980s. As vinyl printing got more sophisticated and affordable, full-blown car skins became prevalent in Japan and even in the West, with otakus with more money than perhaps good taste (or armed with a strong sense of irony) jumping on board. Even major brands have been on the trend in recent years, too. Naturally, since Forza Horizon 6 allows users to generate their own custom designs, Itasha car culture has proliferated within the game as well. However, sometimes the designs have fallen afoul of Forza Horizon's "E for Everyone" rating. Or at least, on paper.      Some of the skins that have caught bans are pretty clearly in violation of the policies like the above, but others seem relatively innocuous, making users wonder if Microsoft is being a bit heavy-handed. One user told me that they had been banned for a month, potentially for the above livery, which they had designed and then kept in storage. I say potentially, because Forza doesn't exactly tell you why you've been banned or for which livery. "This game has a forum for appealing penalties, and although I submitted a post there, I haven't received a reply in over a month," he said. "Consequently, I have no idea which livery caused my ban." "Furthermore, there are people who received harsher penalties than I did—such as permanent bans or device bans—despite creating vinyls featuring female characters that were clearly less revealing than mine." Other livery creators have seen their entire Xbox accounts permanently banned without so much of an explanation. If you live in the U.S. or UK and have ever had to deal with Microsoft's Kafka-esque AI-powered support systems, imagine how much worse they are outside of Microsoft's core markets. There's little viable recourse to appeal bans, seemingly, and Microsoft's systems aren't transparent enough about the reasons as to why a user might catch a ban, permanent or temporary. speculated that Forza Horizon is using some form of auto-banning system, AI-powered or otherwise, handing out false bans. Forza Horizon's Code of Conduct claims that all reports are reviewed by a human moderator and now contains a segment regarding "Itasha-style" designs. "Itasha-style designs are permitted; however, explicit sexual content and sexually suggestive content are forbidden. While we cannot show specific examples of suggestive imagery in this article, designs that depict provocative poses, associated gestures and facial expressions, and attention to specific body parts can be examples of suggestive imagery." The problem here could pertain to a lack of "specific examples" more than likely. When it comes to art, what could be deemed "sexually suggestive" is subjective across cultures and demographics. But it also continues a general trend of Microsoft's opaque systems for enforcement across its platforms. A former Xbox staffer told me that the teams that handle moderation within Forza and other games had effectively been gutted by Microsoft's layoffs, leaving a big gap for community management in general across Microsoft's platforms. Indeed, even beyond the Itasha ban waves, I've been investigating hacked Xbox users being locked out of their accounts due to the way Microsoft handles account support for Xbox as well, and the above could just be symptomatic of overstretched staff unable to handle the workload placed upon them.      Microsoft has struggled to get Xbox stock to its main markets, let alone some of its smaller markets like Europe, the Middle East, and indeed, Japan itself. But there's a cultural issue too. Microsoft generally doesn't make or publish games that have strong appeal outside of its U.S.-centric markets, and Japanese publishers have historically arrived on Xbox last. The situation has improved over time with companies like Square Enix, Capcom, and Konami pledging greater support, but I would argue things still aren't where they should be. Forza Horizon 6 is currently Xbox exclusive, and if the RAMpocalypse wasn't destroying stock levels, it might've been a good source of progress for the brand in Japan. Regardless, the situation with the Itasha liveries highlights, again, Microsoft's opaque systems for enforcement and account management. Over the summer, a Brazilian user who was locked out of his account by a hacker actually sued Microsoft and won after the big M admitted he was hacked but claimed they couldn't do anything about it. Since then, Xbox has been working through a backlog to help users locked out of their accounts to regain access, but it shouldn't be this hard. As more of our content goes digital, and with AI-powered mods and user-generated art becoming more commonplace, the systems that govern access to our digital platforms need to improve a ton. Losing access to years of content and hundreds or thousands of dollars of investment shouldn't come without a clear explanation of why you lost access. Nor should appealing those bans be so slow and difficult. It'll probably end with some form of legislation, but that won't help today's users. 21.10.2026  Johannes Gottwald 				 				 (Senior Editor)			  A common launch month for a self-published thriller looks like this: $250 on social ads, $200 on the retailer’s own sponsored listings, $150 for a spot in a deals newsletter, and about 400 copies sold. Ask the author which of those dollars sold the books and the honest answer is usually a shrug. So the next launch gets the same budget, split the same way. Indie authors have more tools than ever for writing and promoting. Fewer of them have a clear picture of what any of it returns. Table of Contents Ads can get a reader to page one. Typos and inconsistencies decide whether they buy book two, and readers say so in reviews. Many fiction writers go looking for Grammarly alternatives because general-purpose grammar checkers treat fiction like office email. They flag sentence fragments in dialogue, rewrite a character’s dialect into standard English, and question every invented name. The tools that work better for novelists let you load a style sheet with character names and spellings, switch off rules for dialogue, and check consistency across a full manuscript, catching the detective whose eyes are gray in chapter three and brown in chapter nineteen. Accepting suggestions in bulk is the classic mistake. A clipped, hard-boiled narrator turns into polite business prose one click at a time. Use AI as a second pass after your own revision, and on a debut, pay a human proofreader anyway. Check the terms before uploading, too; some services reserve the right to use submitted text for training. AI drafts are useful for generating ten headline variations for an ad test in a few minutes. They’re weaker at sounding like the genre. Romance readers know their tropes, and a blurb that says "a journey of love and self-discovery" reads as filler to them. Feed the tool the specific tropes, enemies to lovers, small town, second chance, and rewrite the result yourself. Test two or three versions at a time with small budgets, and keep the cover image the same so you’re only measuring the words. The core problem is that the big retailers share very little about where a buyer came from. Sales show up in your dashboard with no note saying they arrived from a newsletter link. Attribution tracking software closes part of that gap. Each channel gets its own tagged link, so clicks are counted separately, and some retailers offer programs that report sales from outside traffic back to specific links. Combined with a simple log of when each promotion ran, you can usually see which spend lines up with a jump in daily sales. It will undercount. A reader who clicks on a phone and buys on an e-reader two days later often vanishes from the data, and pages read through a subscription library rarely tie back to a click at all. Treat the numbers as directional. Series authors should judge ads on read-through, not the first sale. A first book priced at 99 cents loses money on almost every ad. If 40 percent of those readers buy book two and 30 percent buy book three, the same ad may be one of your best. Once a week, log date, channel, spend, clicks, sales, and pages read. Set a cutoff before you start: if an ad spends three times a book’s royalty without a sale, pause it. Newsletter promos are the exception, since their effect lands in a single day; judge them on that day’s sales alone. The writing gets most of an author’s attention, as it should. But a book finds readers through hundreds of small decisions about money, and the authors who last tend to be the ones who learned to read a spreadsheet almost as closely as a manuscript. As I write this on Vijayadashmi day, I remember the legend that even as Ravana lay dying, Lord Rama asked his brother Lakshmana to sit at his feet as a disciple and get knowledge. In the same spirit, I am sharing insights from George Soros’ long record as a successful trader and investor—the very person many in India love to hate. In fact, whenever anyone has asked me whether even after recognizing a bubble one can play it and get out in time, my answer has been that the only person who has managed to do that more than once at scale is Soros. Others are one-trick ponies who may have been permanently bearish or bullish and got lucky that one time. Soros’ basic insight was that unlike what has been the conventional wisdom, markets are not efficient. When I came into markets over three decades ago, the efficient market theory was the prevailing wisdom being taught in every university—that all available information is already there in asset prices, markets tend to move towards equilibrium and that deviations occur in a random fashion and can be attributed to extraneous shocks. It was clear to me right away that this did not hold in real life. Think about it: if the price of a stock moves from ₹100 to ₹150 in a quarter when no new information has come, which of the two prices is the efficient one? A beloved offshoot of this theory is the calculation of ‘beta,’ which measures how much a stock moves when the market moves by a certain percentage. Again, if you calculate this for each stock, you will find that the beta changes all the time and can hardly be used to predict anything. Soros’ insight went a step further to say that not only are markets inefficient, they are inefficient in certain predictable ways. His framework rests on two cardinal principles. One, market prices distort underlying fundamentals, ranging from negligible to significant deviations. Two, reflexivity, which means that not only do fundamentals determine market prices, but through feedback loops, especially via leverage like debt and equity, the underlying fundamentals can be altered. Sometimes this is simple. For example, in a cyclical industry like cement or steel, when the cycle turns up, the worst company gives you the biggest stock market pop because a small operating margin improvement becomes a big change in its net profit and hence share price. Then the company usually raises capital at the higher stock price, reducing debt and making its financials look even better. The stock price reflexively changes the fundamentals. This is a relatively benign example, but when this happens at scale across a market, it can cause a bubble. ​According to Soros, every market bubble comprises an underlying real-world trend and a prevailing misconception that reinforce each other. They progress through four distinct stages. The inception is when an underlying trend and a misconception turn mutually reinforcing. In most bubbles, there is an underlying trend to start with. Then this mutual reinforcement accelerates if the bubble survives initial negative feedback tests. In a real estate bubble, for instance, the misconception can be that not only are property prices rising, there is no problem with credit because the loans are secured against real estate. This does not recognize the fact that property prices are themselves largely dependent on the easy availability of credit. So, it becomes a self-reinforcing loop. Also, leverage does not only mean excess debt in the system. It can also be over investment and over valuation on the equity side. The latter is largely what happened during the internet boom. Before that, in the 1960s, the US had a conglomerate boom, with companies acquiring others to artificially boost earnings per share, fuelled by inflated stock prices until reality collapsed expectations. Currently, this is most evident in the artificial intelligence (AI) space, where equity valuations have long lost touch with reality and an estimated $1 trillion of credit has also gone in to fund AI. Anthropic, a leader in the field, is borrowing in dollars at over 10%. After the acceleration in the boom comes the twilight period, when expectations diverge wildly from reality and doubts grow, but the momentum persists out of inertia; and when CEOs are telling themselves “to keep dancing until the music stops,” as was said during the mortgage boom before the global financial crisis of 2008-09. This is a suspended animation sort of period. Finally, reality catches up, triggering a sharp bust. Prices typically go even below fair value due to forced liquidations and financial panic. The pendulum swings the other way. During the global financial crisis, the BSE Sensex fell from a peak of 21,206 in January 2008 to 8,160 in March 2009—A decline of about 61%. The fact that markets are neither self-regulating nor in equilibrium makes a case for regulatory intervention. Regulators must actively work to prevent bubbles from growing too large, rather than assume that markets are always right. Indeed, financial crises typically become the impetus for regulatory reform. For example, the US Securities and Exchange Commission came into being as a result of the Great Depression. Since 2019, Thor Industries has been the world's largest RV manufacturer thanks in no small part to its purchase of European giant Erwin Hymer Group. Following the lead of its acquired European brands (not to mention American market trends), Thor has spent much of that same time period expanding out its lineup of camper vans, sold under its eponymous motor coach brand and other group marques. Now it's following another cue from Europe in moving further into the Class B+ segment of motorhomes that run slightly larger than vans without giving up flexibility. The all-new Ford-powered Rize+ debuts as a nimble, broad-shouldered shuttle-home for adventure-curious road-trippers and semi-permanent nomads.  Thor Motor Coach rapidly grew out its lineup of camper vans while the Class B segment was running white hot through much of the 2020s. The brand went from having a 2019 camper van line of exactly zero models to building out a 2026 family of eight different camper van models with 26 floor plan options. It all started with the Sequence van the company previewed in 2019 ahead of an MY2020 launch.  Nothing lasts forever, though, so as the RV market hit the brakes hard, Thor and its competitors began tweaking their product offerings to attract those customers who remain in "buy" mode. And one reliable way of making any product more desirable is by increasing its value proposition, offering more of what people want for less price. In this case, RV manufacturers are starting to package the lower buy-in pricing and increased interior space of Class C motorhomes into compact, flexible footprints more akin to camper vans.  In other words, they're pushing a new generation of Class B+ motorhomes, versatile 'tweeners that can meet the needs of many different types of buyers: first-time RV owners, off-road adventurers with loads of gear, couples, families and more. In place of the fixed spaces of B+ and C motorhomes of old, this new generation relies more on camper van-inspired convertible spaces and furniture.  With that market backdrop in mind, the Rize+ launches as Thor's answer to the Winnebago's own new, affordable Class B+ series – the Elora/Resa. And since Winnebago already laid all its cards on the table, Thor uses the launch as an opportunity to undercut Winnebago's offfering, both in terms of manufacturer pricing and sizing. The Rize+ measures in at the same 19.7 feet (6 m) length as some of Thor Motor Coach's mid-length camper vans, making for a nimbler, more maneuverable van-like driving and parking experience than big, long, bulky Class C products can ever offer. Instead of following Winnebago's lead with a common Ram Promaster chassis, Thor reaches for the Ford E-Series chassis. But unlike its competition at Forest River, it doesn't sculpt a sleek, modernized compact Class A from the stripped chassis up, instead leaning into the boxy styling of the cab on the E-Series Cutaway Chassis.  Beyond the sculpted fairing above the cab, Thor's Rize+ RV module is as boxy as the Ford nose, increasing livable volume. At 7.1 feet (216 cm) wide, not including the side mirrors, it measures 4 inches (10 cm) wider than Thor's camper vans and doesn't taper inward toward the roof, further maximizing interior volume. Thor's aluminum tube-framed vacu-bonded composite construction isn't as effortlessly sleek and stylish as something like Rossmönster's more sculpted Loft motorhome, but it makes for a handsome, well-proportioned little motorhome in its own right, an RV that looks ready to get lost and stay there.  Thor keeps things simpler than its aforementioned rivals at Coachmen and Winnebago, skipping the foldaway rear benches in favor of fixed vis-a-vis sofas that work as their own single beds or transform into a 52 x 82-in (132 x 208-cm) double bed.. Rize+ drivers certainly lose out on expandable garage space without  folding sofas, but the center aisle between the benches still provides space for a bicycle or two, easily loaded through the rear door. A removable table turns the sofas into a dining area.  The single 18R Rize+ floor plan then sees both the kitchen block and bathroom pushed all the way forward behind the two cab seats. The wet bathroom houses a foot-activated flush toilet, sink with dedicated faucet and shower with independent wand. The kitchen across the aisle and comes includes a central sink with roll-up grated cover for drying and rinsing, portable induction cooker, electric door fridge and microwave.  The Rize+ standard features package brings together virtually everything campers will need to stay comfortable year-round: a 3,400-BTU furnace, water heater, 13,500-BTU air conditioner and 100-Ah battery-based electrical system with 100-W solar panel, 1,000-W inverter and backup generator. Fresh water carries in a 77.6-liter tank.  The two-door Ford E-350 Super Duty chassis, meanwhile, brings some serious grunt in the form of a 7.3-liter V8 with 325 hp and 450 lb-ft of torque. The Rize+ only has two sleeping berths but can seat up to four people on the ride via the two cab seats and two vis-a-vis seatbelts on the rear sofas.  The Rize+ starts at an MSRP of $130,340, which is well below the price of any of Thor Motor Coach's camper vans. It's also more than $20K less than the Winnebago Elora/Resa. Like Winnebago, Thor offers a twin model: the Scope+. The two B+ models follow in the footsteps of Thor's twin Rise and Scope camper vans in featuring different interior and exterior appearance options with identical layouts and equipment.
